parts.name: AlertDialog
parts.description: Holds the open state. Control it with `open` and `onOpenChange`, or leave it uncontrolled and let the trigger and the buttons do it.

parts.name: AlertDialogTrigger
parts.description: The element that opens the window, usually the button that starts the action. Pass your own button with `render`. Focus returns to it when the window closes.

parts.name: AlertDialogContent
parts.description: The window, with its own portal and backdrop. It has no close button in the corner, so the footer buttons are the way out. `size="lg"` makes it the 440 px width of the Figma set.

parts.name: AlertDialogHeader
parts.description: Stacks the icon, the title and the description at the top of the window.

parts.name: AlertDialogIcon
parts.description: A 40 px tile with the icon above the title, in the `default`, `warning` or `destructive` tint. Without children it shows circle-alert, the warning triangle or trash-2.

parts.name: AlertDialogTitle
parts.description: Names the action and its object, such as `Delete project “Northstar”?`. It is the accessible name of the window.

parts.name: AlertDialogDescription
parts.description: Says what will be lost or cannot be undone. It is read out after the title.

parts.name: AlertDialogFeedback
parts.description: An announced message above the actions, `tone="error"` or `"warning"`: what failed, whether anything changed, what to do next.

parts.name: AlertDialogFooter
parts.description: The row of buttons. The last button in the markup sits on the right, or on top when the footer is stacked.

parts.name: AlertDialogCancel
parts.description: Closes the window without acting. It renders a plain Button; label it with the safe choice, `Cancel` or `Keep editing`.

parts.name: AlertDialogAction
parts.description: Confirms and closes on click. It renders a Button: `primary` by default, `destructive` for removals, or `secondary` for a third way out such as `Discard changes`.

parts.name: AlertDialogOverlay
parts.description: The dimmed, lightly blurred backdrop. AlertDialogContent already renders it. A click on it does nothing.

parts.name: AlertDialogPortal
parts.description: Moves the window to the end of the document. AlertDialogContent already renders it; you only need it for a custom window or a custom `container`.

items.text: Name the object and the loss: `Delete project “Northstar”?` as the title and what goes with it in the description, not `Are you sure?`.
Repeat the action on the confirm button and set `variant="destructive"` for deletions: `Delete project` after `Cancel`, so it ends up on the right.
Label the safe choice with what it does: `Keep editing` or `Cancel`. When the action is hard to undo, focus starts on it.

Control `open` yourself when the action is slow or can fail. `AlertDialogAction` closes the window on click, before any request has finished; call `event.preventBaseUIHandler()` in `onClick` to keep it open, then show the failure with `AlertDialogFeedback` and turn the button into `Retry`.
Ask for a typed confirmation only for large deletions that cannot be undone, with a visible label, and never together with an acknowledgement.
Don't confirm with `window.confirm`. It cannot be styled or tested, while an Alert Dialog keeps the product's look, its focus handling and its button labels.
Don't use an Alert Dialog for a form or to report that something worked. A task with fields belongs in a Dialog, and success in a toast.
Don't ask for confirmation on routine actions that can be undone. Do them and offer Undo; a window for everything teaches people to click through.
Don't rely on a click outside or a close button in the corner to dismiss it. Neither exists here: the footer buttons and Escape are the way out.

parts.description: Holds the open state of one panel and wraps its trigger and the panel. `appearance` is `row` (a full-width trigger row) or `inline` (a link-style trigger that hugs its label); without it the trigger keeps the plus and minus box.

parts.description: The header, a `<button>` with `aria-expanded`. It takes an optional leading `icon`, a `description` second line, a `summary` that shows only while the panel is closed, a `count` badge and an `indicator`. Hover fills with the page tone, pressed with the subtle tone, disabled dims to 40 %.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The optional `icon` before the label. It is decorative and takes the text colour.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The children of the trigger. Name it after what is hidden; it is the accessible name of the button and stays the same when the panel opens.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: The `count` badge after the label. It must equal the number of rows in the panel.

parts.name: Indicator

parts.name: CollapsibleRow
parts.description: Puts a control beside the trigger, never inside it: `action` takes a button such as Edit.

parts.name: CollapsibleContent
parts.description: The panel. It opens on a grid-row transition, so nothing is measured. In the row and inline appearances it sits 24 px below the trigger (16 px when nested) and lines up with the trigger text; `align="title"` lines it up with the label after a leading icon.

parts.name: CollapsibleFeedback
parts.description: The loading, empty and error content of a panel, with an optional action such as Retry.

items.text: Pick `row` for a section header and `inline` for a link-style trigger under running text. Use one `appearance` per group of triggers.
Name the trigger after what is hidden: `Advanced options`, `Shipping details`. Keep the title the same when it opens; only the indicator changes.
Use `summary` for what people need while the panel is closed (`3 items · $84.00`) and `count` for the number of things inside; the count must equal the rows in the panel.
Keep fields a form needs outside the closed panel. A collapsed panel is easy to skip, and an error inside it stays out of sight.
Show loading, empty and error content with `CollapsibleFeedback` and offer an action such as Retry.
Don't put buttons or links inside `CollapsibleTrigger`. It is a `<button>` itself; put an action beside it with `CollapsibleRow`.
Don't nest more than one level. For deeper structures use a tree view or separate pages.
Don't add a height transition to `CollapsibleContent`. It already opens on `grid-template-rows` with motion tokens, and a second animation fights it.
Don't stack several collapsibles to build an FAQ or a settings list. That is an Accordion, which also closes the open row.

parts.name: Meter
parts.description: The root: a `div` with `role="meter"`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax` and `aria-valuenow`. Children such as the label and the value render above the bar.

parts.name: MeterLabel
parts.description: Names what is measured. Meter points `aria-labelledby` at it. Without a label, give Meter an `aria-label`.

parts.name: MeterValue
parts.description: Prints the formatted value at the right, a percent of the range by default, in tabular figures. It is hidden from assistive technology, because the meter already announces its value.

parts.name: MeterIndicator
parts.description: The fill, in the brand colour. It is drawn at full width and scaled to the value, and it glides to a new value over `duration-ambient`. Meter already renders it.

parts.name: MeterTrack
parts.description: The grey bar behind the fill: 8 px high and fully rounded. Meter already renders it; you only need it for a custom layout.

items.text: Use a Meter for a measured value inside a known range: storage used, a score, a quota. For a task that runs to completion, use Progress.
Name it with `MeterLabel` or `aria-label`. Screen readers announce the value, and without a name they cannot say what it measures.
Set `max` to the real limit and show the unit in the text: `38 of 50 GB`, not a bare `76%`. Use `format` for a unit or the children of `MeterValue` for your own text.
When you print your own text, pass `getAriaValueText` as well, so a screen reader hears the same words: `38 of 50 gigabytes`. Otherwise it announces the percent.
Measure bars that belong together against the same `max`, as in a storage widget, so the fills can be compared.
Say in words what a full or nearly full meter means, and what to do about it: `All seats are in use.`
Don't use Meter for the progress of a task. A meter is read as a measurement, so a half-full upload would look like a fixed value. Use Progress.
Don't expect the fill to change colour near the limit. Meter has no low, high or optimum ranges; tell the person in the text.
Don't animate the width of the fill yourself. The fill already moves with a transform on the `duration-ambient` timing, which is cheaper and matches the other bars.

components.title: Kbd
components.description: Displays a keyboard key or shortcut, e.g. inside a search input.

parts.name: Kbd
parts.description: One key chip, a `<kbd>` element 22 px high with a subtle fill, a border and a 4 px corner. It holds a single key (`K`, `Esc`, `/`) or a short combination written as one symbol group such as `⌘K`, and grows with its text from a 20 px minimum width. `tone="inverse"` switches to the 18 px dark chip with white text for dark surfaces such as tooltips.

parts.name: KbdGroup
parts.description: Lines up several keys in a row with a 4 px gap. `tone` is passed on to every direct `Kbd` child that has no tone of its own, and `separator` is drawn between two keys.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: The text between two keys, drawn from the `separator` prop of `KbdGroup`: a plus for a combination, a word such as `then` for a sequence. It is muted on a light surface and white on the inverse tone, and there is none after the last key.

items.text: Use Kbd to show a keyboard shortcut next to the action it triggers: in a menu item, a command palette, a tooltip, a search field or a shortcuts panel.
Put one key in each `Kbd` and join keys with `KbdGroup`. Use `separator="+"` when the keys must read as one combination, such as `Ctrl + Shift + P`, and a word such as `then` for a sequence.
Write the keys the way the platform labels them: `⌘`, `⇧` and `⌥` on macOS, `Ctrl`, `Shift` and `Alt` on Windows. Keep one platform per list.
Use `tone="inverse"` when the shortcut sits on a dark surface, and set it on the `KbdGroup` so every key follows. A `Kbd` wrapped in another element does not receive the group's tone.
Set `aria-keyshortcuts` on the control the shortcut triggers. The chip is text for the eye; the attribute tells assistive technology.
Don't use Kbd for decoration or for text that is not a key. It is a hint, not a button, and it does not run the shortcut.
Don't list a shortcut that the app does not handle. A hint that does nothing erodes trust in every other hint.
Don't mix platforms in one list, such as `⌘S` next to `Ctrl+F`. Read the platform and show one set.

aria: role=status with aria-label "Loading" — pass your own label when more specific

parts.name: Spinner
parts.description: A Lucide loader icon that turns once a second. It is 16 px and muted by default, has the `status` role and the name `Loading`, and takes its size and colour from `className`. Pass `aria-label` to say what is loading, or `aria-hidden` when a visible text already does.

items.text: Use a Spinner for a short wait tied to an action: a status line that saves, a panel that refreshes. When content with a known layout loads, use a Skeleton.
Pass a specific `aria-label`, such as `Saving changes`, when the spinner stands alone. The default `Loading` says nothing about what is happening.
Beside a visible text, hide the spinner with `aria-hidden` and put `role="status"` on the text, so the change is announced once and not twice.

Match the size to what is next to it: `size-4` for body text, `size-6` for a row icon, `size-8` for a panel. Use `text-primary` for a wait the person started and keep the muted default for background work.
Keep the space the spinner takes when it goes away, so the layout does not move: give its row a fixed height or swap it for an icon of the same size.
Don't put a Spinner inside a Button. A button has `pending` for that: it draws the spinner, keeps its width and blocks a second press.
Don't swap a chart or a list for a Spinner while it loads. The area collapses and the layout jumps; use a Skeleton of the same size.
Don't use a Spinner when you know how far along the task is. Show a Progress bar, so people can tell whether it is worth waiting.

items.text: Use a Toolbar for a set of controls that act on one thing, such as the formatting buttons of an editor or the tools of a canvas. For joined buttons that switch a view, use a Button Group.
Name the toolbar with `aria-label`, such as `Text formatting`, and every icon-only ToolbarButton with its own `aria-label`.
Sort the buttons into ToolbarGroups with a ToolbarSeparator between them, so related actions sit together and the arrow keys still pass through the whole row.
Show a tooltip with the name and the shortcut on every icon button, and put the tooltips of one toolbar in one `TooltipProvider` so they share a delay.
Keep a toolbar to one row of 4 to 12 items. When more tools are needed, move the ones used least behind an overflow button instead of letting the row scroll.
Don't add your own arrow-key handling or `tabIndex` to the items. The toolbar already moves focus between them, and Tab leaves it.
Don't put a menu, a select or a field in place of a button without checking it with the keyboard. Only buttons, links and inputs of the toolbar take part in its roving focus.
Don't use a Toolbar for navigation between pages; use tabs or a navigation bar. A toolbar is for actions on the thing in front of the user.

parts.name: DropdownMenuSub

parts.name: DropdownMenuSubTrigger

parts.name: DropdownMenuRadioItem

parts.name: DropdownMenuSeparator

parts.name: DropdownMenuEmpty

items.text: Name destructive entries after the action and the object, and set `variant="destructive"`: `Delete project`, not `Delete`. The colour is a second cue, never the only one.
Put the destructive entry last, after a separator, and the most used entries first.
Disable an entry that does not apply right now instead of removing it. Arrow keys still reach it, so screen reader users learn that the action exists.
Show `DropdownMenuLoading` while entries load and `DropdownMenuEmpty` when there are none, with `aria-busy` on the content while loading. The menu never opens as an empty box.
Put the shortcut in `DropdownMenuShortcut` and the binding in `aria-keyshortcuts`, so the entry is read as `Copy`, not `Copy ⌘C`.
Don't put links to pages in a Dropdown Menu. It is a menu of actions; navigation belongs in the navbar menu or in plain links.
Don't use it to pick a value for a form field. A Native Select or a Combobox shows the chosen value in the field itself.
Don't pile up entries. Past seven or eight, split the menu into labelled groups, and never nest more than one submenu.

items.text: Give the trigger an `href` to the full page. A click, a tap and a screen reader still get there, and the preview stays an extra.
Keep the content to a summary that fits the fixed width: an avatar, a name and one or two lines, or a title with a status.

parts.description: Holds the open state and links the trigger to the panel. Control it with `open` and `onOpenChange`, or leave it uncontrolled. `modal` decides whether the page behind the panel stays usable. Renders nothing itself.

items.text: Give the panel a clear job: one short form, one list of options, or one question with its buttons. Keep a title and a line of text so people know what they opened.
Set a width with `className`, such as `w-64`. Without it the panel is as wide as its widest line.
Close the panel with `PopoverClose` around Cancel and Apply, so the focus goes back to the trigger.
Put the trigger where people expect the content to belong, and use `align` so the panel stays inside the page at the edge of the screen.
Don't put a long form, a table or a multi-step task in a popover. Use a Dialog or a side panel when people need the room.
Don't use it for a short label on an icon. A Tooltip is for that, and it needs no click.
Don't open one popover from inside another. Move the second choice into the first panel.
Don't hide the only way to do something in a popover that opens on hover. Touch screens cannot hover, so keep the click.

items.text: Name the table with a `TableCaption`, or with an `aria-label` on Table when the page heading already does. When the table scrolls sideways, that name also labels the scroll region.
Align numbers to the right and set them in `tabular-nums`, so figures line up and do not shift when they change. Right-align the column heading too. Text stays left.
Give amounts and quantities their unit. `CurrencyCell` adds the currency; for other figures the column heading names the unit.
Show a missing value as an em dash and give screen readers the words `No value`. An empty cell reads as a mistake, and a 0 says something the data does not.
Keep the header when a table loads, is empty or fails, and put the state where the rows go. The columns stay in place, so nothing jumps when the rows arrive.
Don't add row padding or heights by hand. The rows read `--row-py`, so the table follows the density setting.
Don't make a row clickable when nothing inside it is. A row has no focus ring and no keyboard action; put a link or a button in the first cell and let it carry the action.
Don't stack more than a handful of columns on a phone. A table that scrolls sideways hides its right-hand columns; choose the few that matter or use a list.
Don't build sorting, filters or paging by hand around a Table. When people need them, move up to Data Grid or Data Table, which keep that state for you.

props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: value
props.description: The value of the Tab.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Whether the Tab is disabled. If a first Tab on a `<Tabs.List>` is disabled, it won't initially be selected. Instead, the next enabled Tab will be selected. However, it does not work like this during server-side rendering, as it is not know…

props.name: nativeButton
props.description: Whether the component renders a native `<button>` element when replacing it via the `render` prop. Set to `false` if the rendered element is not a button (for example, `<div>`).

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

keyboard: Arrow keys: move between tabs (loops at the ends)
Enter / Space: activate the focused tab (activateOnFocus is false by default)
Tab: from the tab list into the panel
aria: role=tablist / tab / tabpanel with aria-selected and aria-orientation

parts.name: Tabs
parts.description: Holds the selected tab and the orientation, `horizontal` or `vertical`. It is the container of the list and the panels: horizontal puts the list above the panel, vertical beside it.

parts.name: TabsList
parts.description: The `tablist`: a row of tabs in the `default` look (bordered buttons, `shape` rounded or pill) or the `line` look (an underline). It takes a `size` of `sm`, `md` or `lg` and scrolls sideways when the tabs do not fit.

parts.name: TabsTrigger
parts.description: One tab, a button with the `tab` role. Its `value` connects it to the panel with the same value. It holds a label, an icon with a label, or a label with a count.

parts.name: TabsIndicator
parts.description: The underline of the selected tab. In the `line` look each tab draws its own underline, so the grey baseline never moves; `TabsIndicator` is a separate gliding underline for custom layouts.

parts.name: TabsContent
parts.description: The panel shown while its tab is selected. It is a `tabpanel` named by its tab and can take keyboard focus.

items.text: Write short labels in sentence case, one or two words: `Billing history`, not `Billing History`.
Keep every tab in a row the same kind: all labels, all icons with labels, or all with counts.
Set `defaultValue`, or `value`, so a tab is selected from the start. Keep `value` in state or in the URL when people should be able to come back to a tab.
Give the list an `aria-label`, such as `Project sections`, when a page has more than one row of tabs.
Keep the number of tabs small enough for a phone. The row scrolls sideways when it runs out of room, and a tab past the edge is easy to miss.
Don't use tabs to move between pages. Links that change the route are navigation with `aria-current="page"`, not a tablist.
Don't add your own key handlers to the triggers. The arrow keys, Home and End already move between tabs, and Tab moves on into the panel.
Don't set heights on the list or the triggers. Pick a `size` (`sm`, `md`, `lg`): the heights follow the density tokens and match the Button sizes.
Don't hide what people must read or do in a tab they may never open. Required information belongs outside the tabs.

components.title: Agenda
components.description: A time-ordered list of scheduled events.

parts.name: Agenda
parts.description: The bordered, rounded list of `items`, one row each, in the order of the array. It does not sort by time and it takes only `items` and `className`.

parts.name: Row
parts.description: One entry, with 16 px padding and a line below it, except for the last row. Rows are text only, with no click or focus state.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The `time` string as written, in a narrow fixed column on the left. A long value wraps onto a second line.

parts.name: Colour bar
parts.description: A 2 px bar the height of the row, filled with the item's `color`. Without a `color` it takes the primary colour.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title` in semibold text. A long title wraps.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The optional `description` under the title, in smaller secondary text, for a place, a person or a status.

items.text: Use an Agenda for a short, read-only list of what happens when, such as a day's meetings. For past events in order, use Timeline; for rows with guests, a menu or a click action, use Agenda Event.
Sort `items` by time before you pass them in. The list renders them in array order and never reorders.
Write `time` in one short format across the list, such as `09:30`. The time column is 56 px wide, so a range such as `09:00 – 10:30` wraps onto a second line.
Set `color` to a CSS variable such as `var(--brand-secondary)`, not a hex. The value goes straight into an inline style, and only a token follows the theme and dark mode.
Say what an entry is in its `title` or `description`, such as `Cancelled` or `Review`. The bar is only a colour; it does not reach people who cannot tell the hues apart.
Don't make the Agenda clickable by wrapping it in a link or button. Its rows have no hover or focus state; use Agenda Event with `onClick` when an entry opens something.
Don't put the Agenda inside another bordered card. It already draws its own border and background, so a second box doubles the lines.

components.title: Action Bar
components.description: A bar of bulk actions for a selection. It sits where you place it, so fix it to the bottom of the page yourself if it should float.

parts.name: ActionBar
parts.description: The bar: a flex row with a border, a card background, a medium radius and a large shadow. It neither positions nor animates itself, so place it where it belongs, for example in a slot above a list or at the bottom of a table card.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The `label`, such as `3 selected`, set in 14 px medium text. Without a label the separator goes too.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: A 1 px vertical line between the label and the actions, drawn by the bar when there is a label.

parts.name: Actions
parts.description: The `children`, laid out in one row with an 8 px gap. Use small plain buttons and icon buttons; the bar has 8 px of padding on the right so an icon button at the end sits evenly.

items.text: Use an Action Bar for bulk actions on rows someone has selected: export, archive, delete. For actions that are always available, use Toolbar.
Show the bar only while something is selected and put the count in `label`: `3 selected`. The count tells people what the buttons will act on.
Keep to two to four actions that all make sense for any selection. Put the destructive one last.
Give icon-only buttons in the bar an `aria-label`. The bar has no role or name of its own, so each button has to carry its own name.
Place the bar yourself: in a slot above the list, or fixed and centred near the bottom of the view. Keep the room it needs, so the content does not jump when the bar appears.
Switch to icon buttons on narrow screens. The bar does not wrap, so a label with three text buttons is wider than a 320 px screen.
Don't run a destructive bulk action straight from the bar. Confirm it in an Alert Dialog that names how many items go: `Delete 3 invoices?`.
Don't use the bar for one-off page actions such as Save or Share. Those belong in the page header or a toolbar.
Don't leave the bar on screen when the selection is empty. A bar with `0 selected` and live buttons invites a mistake.

components.title: Carousel
components.description: A horizontally scrollable row of items with arrow controls.

props.name: autoPlay
props.description: Advances one slide every this many milliseconds and starts over after the last one. It stops while the pointer or the keyboard focus is inside, while the tab is hidden and with reduced motion. 0 or undefined turns it off.

props.name: drag
props.description: Drag the slides left or right with the mouse or a pen; touch already swipes. The row follows the pointer and, on release, springs to the nearest slide (a quick flick goes one slide further). Turn it off when the slides hold content that ne…

props.name: index
props.description: The slide the row shows, for dots and thumbnails that control it (controlled).

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name of the scrolling region.

props.name: navigationShape
props.description: Shape of the two arrow buttons: a rounded square or a circle.

props.name: onIndexChange
props.description: Called with the number of the slide the row now shows.

props.name: showArrows
props.description: Show the two arrow buttons. Turn them off when dots or thumbnails do the navigating.

props.name: slideSize
props.description: "auto" keeps every slide at its own width, "full" makes each slide as wide as the row.

keyboard: Tab to the slide strip, then Arrow Left / Right scroll it
Previous / Next buttons stay focusable at the ends (aria-disabled)
aria: role=region with aria-roledescription="carousel" and your label; slide changes are announced politely

parts.name: Carousel
parts.description: The row: a flex container with a previous button, the slide strip and a next button, in that order. It snaps to each slide, takes the width of its parent and pauses `autoPlay` while the pointer or keyboard focus is inside.

parts.name: Previous button
parts.description: A plain icon button on the left, a rounded square or a circle (`navigationShape`). It steps one slide back. On the first slide it stays on screen and focusable but disabled; when nothing overflows it is hidden and keeps its place.

parts.name: Slide strip
parts.description: The focusable region named by `label`. It scrolls with the arrow keys, swipes on touch, drags with a mouse or pen, and announces `Items 2–4 of 6` once a scroll has come to rest.

parts.name: Slide
parts.description: Each child, wrapped in a snap point. Slides keep their own width, or with `slideSize="full"` each one is as wide as the strip.

parts.name: Next button
parts.description: The same icon button on the right. It steps one slide forward and is disabled, not hidden, on the last slide.

items.text: Use a Carousel for a row of similar items that people browse, such as project cards, screenshots or template previews. When every item matters, or the items need comparing, show them in a grid instead.
Set `label` to what the row holds, such as `Recent projects`. It names the region, and the default `Carousel` tells nobody what is inside.
Keep the arrows beside the row. They never sit on top of a card, so a slide can hold its own buttons and links.
Drive dots, thumbnails or a counter through `index` and `onIndexChange` instead of scrolling the strip yourself. The carousel springs to the slide and reports the one in view.
Show how many slides there are: a counter such as `Slide 2 of 5`, dots or thumbnails. A row with arrows alone does not tell people where they are.
Offer a pause button next to `autoPlay`, and use it for images, not text. It already pauses on hover, focus, a hidden tab and reduced motion, but moving slides are hard to read.
Don't put the only way to reach important content inside a carousel. People skip it; a grid shows everything at once.
Don't leave `drag` on when slides hold controls that need the mouse, such as a slider. Set `drag={false}`; touch still swipes.
Don't start `autoPlay` in a dashboard or on a page people read. Moving content competes with the text.

components.title: Empty State
components.description: Placeholder shown when a list or search has no results.

props.name: variant
props.description: Frame style — mirrors the Figma Empty State "Style" variants.

parts.name: EmptyState
parts.description: A centred block of icon, title, description and action. `variant` picks the frame: `dashed` (the default), `outline`, `default` without a frame, or `background` with a muted fill. It fills the width of its container and has 40 px of padding.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The `icon` node, drawn in a round 48 px well with a 24 px icon. Pass a Lucide icon.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title`: one short line on what is missing, such as `No invoices yet`. It renders as a paragraph, not a heading, so it does not change the outline of the page.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The `description` under the title: why the place is empty, or what will appear here.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The `action` node below the text, usually one Button that fills the empty place or undoes the filter. It takes any node, also a row of two buttons or a link.

items.text: Say what is missing, why and what to do next, then offer one action: `No invoices yet`, `Invoices appear here as soon as the first one is sent.` and `New invoice`.
For a search without results, name the query and offer a way out: `No results for “Anders”` with `Clear search`.
For a failure, say what failed and offer the retry as the action: `Couldn't load invoices` with `Try again`. Show the pending state on the button while it runs.
Use the frameless `default` look inside a card or panel that already has a border, and the `dashed` default where the empty state stands on the page.
Put an empty state that appears after typing in a wrapper with `role="status"`, so a screen reader announces the change.
Don't show a bare `No results` line. Without a reason and a next step, an empty place looks broken and leaves people stuck.
Don't use it while data is still loading. A Skeleton shows that something is on its way; an empty state says that nothing is.
Don't offer two equal calls to action. One primary button, with at most a plain secondary one or a link to help.

components.title: File Tree
components.description: An indented list of folders and files: a tree with arrow-key navigation whose folders open and close, and onSelect reports the chosen file or folder.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Accessible name of the tree.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Called when a file or folder is activated (click, Enter or Space).

props.name: selectedId
props.description: The selected node (controlled). Without it the tree keeps its own selection.

keyboard: Tab: into the tree once (focused, selected or first row)
Arrow Up / Down: previous / next visible row; Home / End: first / last row
Arrow Right: open a folder, then into its first child; Arrow Left: close a folder, else go to its parent
Enter / Space: toggle a folder and select it, select a file; a letter jumps to the next row with that initial
aria: role=tree named by aria-label (default "Files"); rows role=treeitem with aria-level and aria-selected, folders aria-expanded
Children in role=group; rows of closed folders are inert and never hold focus

parts.name: FileTree
parts.description: A bordered panel with `role="tree"`, named by `aria-label` (default `Files`), that draws `data` as rows. Top-level folders start open, deeper ones closed. One row is the tab stop; the arrow keys move between the visible rows.

parts.name: Folder row
parts.description: A `treeitem` with `aria-level` and `aria-expanded`, a chevron, a folder icon and the name. Choosing it opens or closes its children and selects it; Right opens it or enters the first child, Left closes it.

parts.name: File row
parts.description: A `treeitem` with a file icon and the name, cut with an ellipsis when it is too long. Choosing it selects it and calls `onSelect`. The selected row has `aria-selected` and a subtle fill.

parts.name: Children
parts.description: The nested rows in a `role="group"`, indented one step per level. While closed they are inert and the arrow keys skip them, so focus never lands inside a closed folder.

items.text: Use a File Tree to show a folder structure people look through, such as the files of a template or an export. For items people search, sort or select in bulk, use Table.
Give every node a unique, stable `id`. It is the React key and the value of `selectedId`, and a reused id mixes up which folders are open.
Mark a folder with a `children` array, even an empty one. A node without `children` is drawn as a file.
Keep the choice in your own state with `selectedId` and `onSelect` when something else on the page depends on it, such as an open file. Without `selectedId` the tree keeps its own selection.
Name the tree with `aria-label` when the page has more than one, such as `Project files`. The default name is `Files`.
Do not use it for multiple selection, drag and drop, renaming or icons per file type. It selects one row at a time and draws the same two icons.
Do not expect it to load children on demand. The tree draws the `data` it gets; a folder that is still loading needs its own placeholder row in `data`.

components.title: Floating TOC
components.description: A table of contents for an article, with a marker that follows the section in view. It does not stick by itself: put it in a `sticky` container to keep it on screen.

props.name: scrollContainer
props.description: The element that scrolls the sections, if it is not the page.

parts.name: FloatingToc
parts.description: A `<nav>` named `On this page` with one link per section. It is not sticky itself; place it in a sticky column.

parts.name: Entry
parts.description: An `<a>` to `#id` for each item, indented 12 px per `depth`. The current one is darker, medium weight and carries `aria-current="location"`.

parts.name: Active marker
parts.description: A 2 px bar on the left line that glides to the current entry. A fainter one previews the entry under the pointer or focus.

items.text: Use a Floating TOC beside a long page with several headed sections, such as documentation or a policy. For switching between separate views, use Tabs.
Give every section an `id` that matches its item. The links and the scroll spy find sections by that `id`, and a missing one is never marked.
Pass `scrollContainer` when the sections scroll inside a panel rather than the page. Otherwise the spy watches the window and the marker stands still.
Put it in a sticky column yourself, for example with `sticky top-24`. The component draws the list and the marker, not its position.
Keep labels short, one line each, and in the order of the page. An entry that wraps pushes the marker out of line with its neighbours.
Do not set `activeId` unless you track the section yourself. A set `activeId` turns the scroll spy off, and the marker stops following the reader.
Do not use it as the main navigation of a site. It lists the sections of one page and highlights where the reader is.

components.title: Holo Card
components.description: A card with a soft glow that follows the mouse.

parts.name: HoloCard
parts.description: A card with a border, 16 px of padding, a 16 px radius and `overflow-hidden`. It holds the pointer position in two custom properties, `--holo-x` and `--holo-y`, and takes `className` for the width.

parts.name: Glow
parts.description: A radial gradient 320 px across, mixed from the primary colour at 25 % and faded out at 70 %. It fades in when the card is hovered and follows the pointer. It ignores pointer events and sits behind the content. The figure keeps it on.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The `children`, placed above the glow. Anything goes: text, an icon tile, a badge, buttons.

items.text: Use a Holo Card to make one or two showcase items stand out, such as a featured plan on a landing page. For everyday content and dashboard tiles, use Card.
Use it once or twice per view. When every card glows, none of them stands out.

Tint the glow by setting `--primary` on a wrapper, not with a gradient of your own. It follows brand and dark mode, and everything inside that uses the primary colour changes with it, a gradient Button included.
Keep the card complete without the glow. It appears only under a mouse pointer, so touch and keyboard users never need it.
Put a real link or Button inside for the action, and give the card its width with `className`.
Do not rely on the glow to show that the card is clickable. It is decoration with no focus state, no role and no tab stop.
Do not expect a tilt or a 3D effect. The card never moves or rotates; only the glow under the pointer changes.

components.title: Item Card
components.description: A generic row card: icon, title, description, meta, action.

parts.name: ItemCard
parts.description: One framed row: a 1 px border, an 8 px corner radius, 12 px of padding and 12 px between its parts, on the card surface. It renders a plain `div` and has no hover, focus or click state of its own.

parts.name: Icon tile
parts.description: A 40 px square with an 8 px radius in the indigo tint, with a 20 px icon in the tint text colour. It shows when you pass `icon`.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title` in 14 px semibold. It is cut to one line with an ellipsis.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The `description` under the title in 13 px secondary text, also cut to one line.

parts.name: Meta
parts.description: A short fact on the right in 12 px tertiary text, such as a size or a date. It never shrinks. A Badge works here too.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: One control at the far right, usually a Button or an icon button. It never shrinks and keeps its own focus and click behaviour.

parts.name: ItemCardGroup
parts.description: A bordered box with a 12 px radius and 8 px of padding that stacks several cards with 8 px between them, for a set that belongs together.

items.text: Use an ItemCard for an object that stands on its own row: a file, a connected app, a project, with one action. For many rows people compare by column, use a Table. For a plain list of rows in one frame, use List View.
Put the action in `action` as a Button or an icon button. The card takes no click handler of its own, so the row itself is not interactive.
Give an icon button an `aria-label` that names its object, such as `More options for Checkout redesign`, so the buttons of a set can be told apart.
Keep `title` and `description` short, or give the full text another way. Both are cut to one line with an ellipsis.
Use `meta` for a short fact with its unit, such as `2.4 MB` or `2d ago`, or for a status Badge.
Don't wrap each ItemCard in a Card. It draws its own border and padding. For a set, use ItemCardGroup.
Don't put more than one control in `action`. Two buttons next to a long title leave no room for the text.

components.title: Timeline
components.description: A vertical sequence of dated, dot-connected events.

props.name: compact
props.description: Smaller dots and text, for milestones and long lists.

props.name: orientation
props.description: "vertical" stacks the entries, "horizontal" lays them out in a row with the time above each dot.

parts.name: Timeline
parts.description: Draws the entries from `items`, stacked in a column or in a row with `orientation`, and joins them with a line. `compact` makes dots, text and gaps smaller. It is a plain `div`, not a list.

parts.name: Dot
parts.description: The marker of an entry: a 24 px circle (16 px when compact) in the `color` of the entry, with the `icon` or a small point inside. An `avatar` replaces it.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title` of the entry in semibold text. It is any React node, so keep it to a short sentence.

parts.name: Timestamp
parts.description: The `timestamp` in small tertiary text, printed as written. It sits next to the title in a column and above the dot in a row.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The `description` under the title, in secondary text, for the detail of the entry.

parts.name: Connector
parts.description: A 1 px line in the border colour that runs from one dot to the next. The last entry has none. It is not numbered in the figure because it runs between two dots.

items.text: Pass a stable `id` for every entry. It is the React key, so a list that grows at the top keeps its rows.
Give every `timestamp` a date or a time with its unit, such as `Nov 9, 09:14` or `3 min ago`. Timeline prints it as written, so format it yourself and use the same style in the whole list.
Say the status in words, in the `title` or the `description`: `Tests failed`, not just a red dot. The colour and the icon are decoration for people who can see them.
Pass dot colours as tokens, such as `var(--success)` or `var(--destructive)`. The glyph inside switches between white and dark so it stays readable on the fill.
Set `compact` for long lists and for a Timeline inside a small card. Dots, text and gaps shrink, so more entries fit.
Don't use a horizontal Timeline for more than four or five entries. Each entry gets an equal share of the width, so a long row squeezes the text.
Don't put long paragraphs, buttons or links in `title` or `description`. For one rich entry with a comment, an object chip or attachments, use a Timeline Event.
Don't write times like `recently` or `a while ago`. People cannot tell which entry came first.

components.title: Widget
components.description: A generic dashboard widget shell: header, body, footer.

parts.name: Widget
parts.description: The frame of one dashboard tile: a bordered card with a 16 px radius, 16 px of padding and 16 px between the header, the body and the footer.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: A row with the title and description on the left and the `action` on the right. It renders only when `title` or `action` is set, so a `description` alone does not show.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title` as an `<h3>` in bold 16 px text, so the heading order stays intact under a page heading of level two.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The `description` under the title, in small secondary text: the period, the scope or the unit of the data.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The `action` at the right end of the header, usually a plain `View all` button or an icon button with an `aria-label`.

parts.name: Body
parts.description: The `children`. The body grows to fill the tile, so in a grid row the footers of tiles with different bodies line up at the bottom.

parts.name: Footer
parts.description: The `footer` below a divider line: a note on the data such as `Updated 2 minutes ago`, or one link.

items.text: Put widgets under a page heading of level two. The title renders as an `<h3>`, so the heading order stays intact.
Keep the header to one `action`, such as a plain `View all` button or an icon button with an `aria-label`. More than one belongs in a menu.
Keep the frame in the loading, empty and error states and swap only the body. The tile keeps its title and its place, and the page does not jump.
Set the width on the box around the Widget, or on `className`. It fills its container, so a grid cell or a `max-w-[360px]` decides how wide it is.
Use the footer for a note about the data or for one link, such as `Updated 2 minutes ago` or `Manage plan`.
Don't set a `description` without a `title` or an `action`. The header is then not rendered and the description does not appear.
Don't put a Card or another bordered box in the body. The Widget is already the frame; use rows, dividers and Progress bars inside it.
Don't use a Widget for content with media, a custom header or one press target for the whole tile. Use a Card.

components.title: Segment
components.description: A single-select toggle group, like a compact tab bar, with a pill or a rounded-corner track.

props.name: activation
props.description: `auto` (default): the arrow keys move focus and choose the option. `manual`: the arrow keys, Home and End only move focus; Enter or Space chooses. Use it where a wrong choice has a cost (a permission, a payment).

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group for screen readers, e.g. "Version".

props.name: shape
props.description: `pill` (default) or `rounded` for the square-cornered version.

props.name: slide
props.description: The selected option's pill slides to the next option instead of switching. It moves with `transform` only (the pill is laid out at its final size and animated from the old one), so it costs no layout, and it stays put when the user prefers…

parts.name: Segment
parts.description: The track: one `div` with `role="tablist"` and your `aria-label`, a grey `bg-muted` bar that is as wide as its options. `size` sets its height (32, 28, 36 or 40 px at the compact density) and `shape` its corners: a full pill, or 8 px with options that are concentric to it (6 px at 2 px padding, 4 px at 4 px padding).

parts.name: Option
parts.description: One `button` with `role="tab"` and `aria-selected`, built from the `options` array. The selected option is the one tab stop. Hover is the page fill, pressed the subtle fill, and a disabled option is dimmed to 40 % and skipped by the keys.

parts.name: Selected pill
parts.description: The white pill behind the selected option, drawn only with `slide`. It is one absolutely placed element that moves from the old option to the new one with `transform`. Without `slide` the selected option paints the same white fill itself.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The element you pass as `icon` in an option, drawn before the label at 14 px (`xs`, `sm`) or 16 px (`md`, `lg`). Give a Lucide icon `strokeWidth={1.5}`. It takes the text colour of its option.

items.text: Use a Segment to switch the view or the scope of one piece of content: day, week, month; list or grid; monthly or yearly. For separate panels of content, use Tabs. For on or off, use a switch.
Keep it to two to five options with one-word or short labels. The track hugs its content, does not wrap and does not scroll, so five long labels are wider than a phone.
Pass `aria-label`, for example `Time range`. It names the tab list; the options only carry their own labels.
Give an icon-only option a visually hidden label such as `List`. The option has no other accessible name.

Pick the `size` by place: `xs` and `sm` inside a card or chart header, `md` and `lg` to line up with a Button. The `md` and `lg` heights follow the density tokens, so they stay level with buttons in compact and comfortable.
Turn on `slide` when the options are neighbours the eye should follow, such as a period. Use the plain switch for a control that changes rarely.
Don't pass a `value` that matches no option. The first enabled option becomes the tab stop, but none of them looks selected.
Don't use a Segment to open panels that have their own content and a URL. It announces itself as a tab list but renders no tab panels; Tabs owns the panels.

parts.name: InlineSelect

parts.name: InlineSelectTrigger
parts.description: A borderless button, 24 px high, with an 8 px corner and 8 px of side padding. It shows the current value and a chevron, fills with the page colour on hover and takes the indigo focus ring. It has no visible label, so give it an `aria-label`.

parts.name: InlineSelectValue
parts.description: The label of the chosen option, in 14 px medium. With a `placeholder` it shows that text in the tertiary colour until an option is chosen. An option with an icon shows the icon and the label side by side.

parts.name: Chevron
parts.description: A small chevron in the tertiary colour. It marks the trigger as a select and is hidden from assistive technology.

parts.name: InlineSelectContent
parts.description: The list, in its own portal. It opens below the trigger, never over it, as wide as the trigger and at least 128 px, with a 12 px corner and 4 px of padding. It scrolls when there is not enough room.

parts.name: InlineSelectItem
parts.description: One option, 32 px high with an 8 px corner. The highlighted option takes the page colour. It can start with an icon.

parts.name: Check
parts.description: A check at the right end of the chosen option. It shows only on the option whose value is selected.

items.text: Give every trigger an `aria-label` that names what is chosen, such as `Sort order` or `Status of WUI-482`. There is no visible label, and the announced value alone does not say what the choice is for.
Write the sentence so that it reads whole with any option: `Show comments from the last 30 days`. Keep option labels to one or two words.
Use it where the choice is a detail of something else: a sort order, a period, a status in a row. The text around it carries the meaning.
Make the value change the content at once, as a filter or a figure does. A select that changes nothing visible reads as broken.
Don't use it as a form field. Without a border it does not look like an input; use Native Select with a label inside a Field.
Don't let long labels push the sentence around. The trigger is as wide as the current label, so text after it moves when the value changes; keep labels about the same length.
Don't use it for a choice with more than about ten options or one that needs search. Use Combobox instead.
Don't hide the only way to change a main setting behind it. Make that setting a visible control.

parts.name: ToggleButton

parts.name: Mark

items.text: Use CheckboxButtonGroup for a few short options that can be combined: text styles, days of the week, filters. For exactly one choice, use RadioButtonGroup; for a long list or options with a description, use Checkbox or Selector Item.

Pick the group by what the options mean, not by how they look. CheckboxButtonGroup is a set of toggles (`aria-pressed`, any number on, including none, Tab visits every button). RadioButtonGroup is one choice (`radio` with `aria-checked`, one tab stop, the arrow keys choose, the choice cannot be cleared).
Keep `value` as `string[]` and update it in `onValueChange`. Wrapping on narrow screens is built in, so no custom breakpoints are needed.
Name the group with a visible label and `aria-labelledby`, or with an `aria-label`. A screen reader announces the name when focus enters the group.
Give every icon-only `ToggleButton` an `aria-label` such as `Bold`. The pressed state is announced, but the icon alone has no name.
Put the error on the group: set `aria-invalid` and write one message under it. Do not repeat the message on every button.
Don't use it for options with a sentence of explanation. A button holds a word or two; use a Checkbox or a Selector Item with a description instead.
Don't set `orientation="vertical"` without stacking the buttons, or the arrow keys will move in a direction the layout does not show.
Don't use it to switch between views or pages. People expect a Segment or Tabs for that.

parts.name: RadioButtonGroup
parts.description: A wrapping row of buttons where exactly one is chosen once the person has chosen, with an 8 px gap. It is a `radiogroup`. `value` is an array with the value of the chosen button. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, and set `aria-invalid` to mark the whole group.

parts.name: ToggleButton
parts.description: One button with its own `value`. Inside this group it is a `radio`: `aria-checked` says whether it is chosen, and a chosen button takes the indigo tint. Icon-only buttons need an `aria-label`.

parts.name: Mark
parts.description: The 16 px radio circle in front of the label, with a 6 px dot while the button is chosen. The button draws it for you when it has a text label, and leaves it out for an icon-only button. The pill shape of the button follows the circle. Pass `indicator={false}` to hide it.

items.text: Use RadioButtonGroup for one choice from a few short options that should be one click away: a billing period, a time range, a text alignment. For options with a description, use Radio Group or Selector Item; for combining options, use CheckboxButtonGroup.
Keep `value` as `string[]` and read the choice from `value[0]`. The array has one entry once a button is chosen and never becomes empty by a press, so no guard against an empty choice is needed.
Name the group with a visible label and `aria-labelledby`, or with an `aria-label`. A screen reader announces the name when focus enters the group.
Give every icon-only `ToggleButton` an `aria-label` such as `Align left`. A screen reader announces the label and whether the radio is chosen; the icon alone has no name.
Choose a sensible default with `defaultValue` when one exists, and show what the choice changes right next to the group.
Use CheckboxButtonGroup, not this group, when people may choose several options or none. The two look alike but behave differently: this one is a radio group, CheckboxButtonGroup a set of toggles.
Don't use two buttons for on and off. A single setting that is on or off is a Switch or a Toggle.
Don't use it for more than about five options or for options that need a sentence of explanation. Use a Radio Group or a Select instead.
Don't use it to switch between views or pages. People expect a Segment or Tabs for that.

components.title: Number Stepper
components.description: A +/- increment control for a bounded numeric value.

props.name: format
props.description: Formats the displayed value, e.g. `(n) => `${n}%``

keyboard: Tab to the Decrease / Increase buttons, Enter / Space to step
aria: role=group; the value is announced politely (aria-live) when it changes
The buttons carry aria-label "Decrease" / "Increase"

parts.name: NumberStepper
parts.description: A `div` with `role="group"` that holds a minus button, the number and a plus button, 8 px apart. It is controlled: you pass `value` and `onValueChange`. It has no visible label, so give it an `aria-label`; it takes the attributes of a `div`.

parts.name: Decrease button
parts.description: A 32 px plain icon button named `Decrease`. At `min` it dims to 40 % but stays focusable (`aria-disabled`), so repeated Enter does not drop focus to the page.

parts.name: Value
parts.description: The number between the buttons, at least 32 px wide, in semibold with tabular figures so it does not jiggle. It shows `format(value)` and is announced politely when it changes.

parts.name: Increase button
parts.description: A 32 px plain icon button named `Increase`. It dims and stops at `max` in the same way.

items.text: Name the group with an `aria-label` such as `Adults` or `Quantity of canvas tote bags`. The buttons only say `Decrease` and `Increase`, and the group name tells a screen reader what they change.
Set `min`, `max` and `step` to the real limits, so the buttons stop where the values stop. The value is clamped; it never leaves the range.
Use `format` to add the unit, for example `(n) => `${n} min``, so the number is not read without it.
Say why a limit was reached when it is not obvious, such as `Only 5 in stock`. A dimmed button alone does not explain itself.
Don't use it for a value people may want to type, such as 250. There is no text entry, so a jump from 1 to 250 takes 249 presses. Use Number Field.
Don't expect the arrow keys to work. It is two buttons, not a spin button: Tab reaches each button and Enter or Space presses it. Use Number Field where arrow keys, Home and End matter.
Don't use it for a range where the position matters more than the number. A Slider shows where the value sits between the limits.
Don't show the number in the stepper and again in a label next to it. One place for the value is enough.
