parts.name: Prompt
parts.description: The line `Drop files here or browse`. It is the visible name of the control.

parts.name: Browse link
parts.description: The word `browse` in the link colour. It is not a separate button: a click anywhere on the zone opens the file dialog.

parts.name: Hint
parts.description: The small line under the prompt. It defaults to the accepted types, or `Any file type`, and is where a size limit belongs. It is the accessible description of the file input.

parts.name: File input
parts.description: The real `<input type="file">`, visually hidden and always `multiple`. It takes the keyboard focus, and the focus ring is drawn around the whole zone.

items.text: State the limit in `hint`, for example `PNG, JPG or PDF up to 10 MB`. The zone does not enforce a size, so say what you will check.
Show every file in a list under the zone, with name, size, a progress bar while it uploads and a Remove or Cancel action. The zone itself shows no files.
Say in words why a file was refused, such as `File type not supported. Use PNG, JPG or PDF.`, and keep the row so people see which file it was.
Check the type and the size of every file in `onFiles`. A drop passes every file, whatever `accept` says.
Don't rely on `accept` to keep wrong files out. It only filters the file dialog; a dropped file of any type reaches `onFiles`.
Don't make drag and drop the only way in. The zone also opens the file dialog on a click and on Enter or Space, and your page should keep that path working.
Don't put the zone inside another clickable element, such as a button or a link. It is already a label around an input, and the click would count twice.
Don't use it for a single file in a tight form row. A Button that opens the file dialog takes less room and reads as a form control.

components.title: Rich Text Editor
components.description: A Tiptap-powered WYSIWYG editor with a formatting toolbar.

props.name: aria-describedby
props.description: Id of the element that describes the editing area, such as a helper line.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Accessible name of the editing area when there is no visible label.

props.name: aria-labelledby
props.description: Id of the element that names the editing area, such as a visible label.

props.name: id
props.description: Id of the editing area. A `<label htmlFor>` cannot name it (it is not a form control): use `aria-labelledby`.

parts.name: RichTextEditor
parts.description: A 16 px frame with a 1 px border that holds the toolbar and the editing area. It loads its engine (Tiptap) the first time it renders and shows a skeleton until then. `content` is the starting HTML and `onChange` receives the whole document as HTML after every edit. The frame takes the indigo border and the ring when the text has focus.

parts.name: RichTextEditorSkeleton
parts.description: The empty frame with the placeholder that shows until the editor has loaded, 38 px of toolbar and 128 px of text. Export it for your own loading state.

parts.name: Toolbar
parts.description: A row of 28 px icon buttons in 6 px of padding with a 2 px gap, closed off from the text by a 1 px line: Bold, Italic, Underline, Bulleted list, Numbered list and Link.

parts.name: Toolbar button
parts.description: A 28 px icon button with an 8 px corner and a 16 px icon. It has an `aria-label` and `aria-pressed`, so it is a toggle: pressed, with the subtle fill, while the cursor is in text that has the format. Link asks for the address in the browser's prompt.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: A 1 px line, 20 px high, between the text styles, the lists and the link.

parts.name: Editing area
parts.description: The editable text: a multi-line `textbox` at least 128 px tall with 12 px of padding, that grows with its content. While it is empty it shows the `placeholder`. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

items.text: Use a Rich Text Editor for text that people format: a note, a project description, a reply, release notes. For plain text use a Textarea; for a message to an AI assistant use a Prompt Input.

Name the editing area. Use `aria-labelledby` with the id of a visible `Label`, or `aria-label` when there is no room for a label. A `<label htmlFor>` cannot reach it, because the area is not a form control.

Store the HTML from `onChange` and pass it back as `content` when the person comes back. `content` is the starting text only, so later changes to the prop do not replace what was typed. Use a new `key` to load other content.
Sanitize the HTML on your server before you store it or show it to other people. The editor limits the tags it produces, but a server should never trust the browser.
Say what is wrong next to the editor and keep the text. The editor has no invalid state of its own: colour the frame with `border-error` and describe the problem with `aria-describedby`.

Don't use it for text that must stay plain, such as a name, a title or a search term. The output is HTML (`

`, ``), not plain text, and a one-line Input is easier to fill in.
Don't use it as the composer of an AI chat. That is a Prompt Input: it sends on Enter, grows with the message and has attach and send buttons, not a formatting toolbar.
Don't rely on a shortcut for the link. There is none: the toolbar button is the way to add or remove a link.

components.title: Color Picker
components.description: Pick a colour: saturation and brightness, hue, opacity, eyedropper, HEX/RGB/HSL values and saved colours — inline or from a trigger field.

props.name: alpha
props.description: Opacity, 0–1. Leave out `onAlphaChange` and `alpha` to hide the opacity slider.

props.name: format
props.description: The value fields' format; the select in the picker switches it.

props.name: onClose
props.description: Shows the close button.

props.name: swatches
props.description: Saved colours; the + adds the current colour.

props.name: title
props.description: Heading of the panel. Hidden when `null`.

props.name: value
props.description: The colour as #RRGGBB.

props.name: variant
props.description: How a colour is picked: a saturation/brightness area or a grid of swatches.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Whether the popover is open by default.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name of the field.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.description: Called when the popover opens or closes.

props.name: open
props.description: The popover is open. Controlled; leave out for the field to manage it.

props.name: pickerProps
props.description: Everything else the picker takes (alpha, swatches, format …).

props.name: shape
props.description: `default`: the Input-sized field with a square swatch. `pill`: a 32 px pill with a colour dot, to sit in a row of pill-shaped colour presets.

keyboard: Arrow keys: move the saturation/brightness handle and the hue slider
aria: The handles are role=slider with aria-valuetext; swatches are options in a listbox

parts.name: ColorPicker
parts.description: The panel: a 296 px wide card with a title, a colour area, hue and opacity sliders, the value fields and a row of saved colours. It holds the colour as `#RRGGBB` and the opacity as a number from 0 to 1. Everything is reachable from the keyboard, and it is not a native colour input.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: The title, `Color picker` by default, and with `onClose` a close button at the right. `title={null}` removes the title and, without `onClose`, the whole header.

parts.name: Colour area
parts.description: A slider in two dimensions: saturation runs left to right and brightness bottom to top, on the current hue. With `variant="grid"` it becomes a grid of greys and nine shades of twelve hues, where the arrow keys move from swatch to swatch.

parts.name: Hue and opacity
parts.description: Two sliders under the area, with an eyedropper button at the left in browsers that have one. The opacity slider and field are left out with `showAlpha={false}`.

parts.name: Value
parts.description: A select for the format (HEX, RGB or HSL) and the fields for the value, followed by the opacity in percent. A field commits on Enter or blur, so typing `2` on the way to `255` does not move the colour.

parts.name: Saved colours
parts.description: A row of 24 px swatches with a plus button that saves the current colour. The chosen swatch gets a ring in its own colour. `defaultSwatches` sets the first set and `swatches` with `onSwatchesChange` controls it.

parts.name: ColorPickerTrigger
parts.description: A field that opens the picker in a popover below it: a swatch, the hex value and a chevron, the size of an Input. `shape="pill"` makes it a 32 px pill with a colour dot, for a row of colour presets. Its accessible name is the `label` followed by the value.

items.text: Use `ColorPickerTrigger` in a form or a settings row. The field shows the colour at rest, and the panel opens only when it is needed.
Use `ColorPicker` on the page when the colour is the task, for example an editor with a preview beside it. Judge the colour on real content, not on a bare swatch.

Hold the colour as `#RRGGBB` with `value` and `onValueChange`, and the opacity as a number with `alpha` and `onAlphaChange`. Leave opacity out with `showAlpha={false}` where a colour is always opaque.
Pass the colours of your product as `defaultSwatches`, so people start from a palette they should use.
Give the trigger a `label`, such as `Primary colour`. Its accessible name is the label and the value, because the swatch alone says nothing to a screen reader.
Don't use a native `<input type="color">`. Its panel is the browser's own and cannot carry your tokens, your saved colours or an opacity.
Don't use a colour as the only information. A picked colour needs its value in text, as the field and the preview line show.
Don't use it to choose from a short list of fixed colours. A row of Selector Items or a Radio Button Group is quicker and keeps people inside your palette.

components.title: Cell Color Picker
components.description: A compact color swatch picker for inline use in a Data Grid cell.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Name for screen readers, such as "Label colour". The accessible name becomes "Label colour, #6366F1". Default: "Colour #6366F1. Choose a colour".

parts.name: Table
parts.description: The table the cell sits in. Its first column holds the row names and its header row names the columns. The cell control is a child of a `TableCell`.

parts.name: Column header
parts.description: The `TableHead` of the colour column. It says what the colour is for, such as Colour or Chart colour.

parts.name: Row header
parts.description: The first cell of the row, marked `role="rowheader"`. It says which label, calendar or series this colour belongs to. Pass the same name as `aria-label` on the swatch so it is announced on its own.

parts.name: CellColorPicker
parts.description: A round swatch button that opens a six-colour popover. It is built for a table cell and returns the chosen colour as a hex string. It is controlled: you hold `value` and write it back in `onValueChange`.

parts.name: Swatch button
parts.description: The 24 px round trigger, filled with the current colour, with a 1 px border ring and a 2 px gap. It is named by `aria-label` and the hex value, or by `Colour #12AFF0. Choose a colour` without a label, and announces a dialog.

parts.name: Popover
parts.description: The popover named by the `aria-label` (default `Choose a colour`), with the six swatches in one row of 8 px padding. It stays open after a choice.

parts.name: Swatch
parts.description: One of the six colour buttons of the popover, named by its hex value. The active one has `aria-pressed` and a ring.

items.text: Keep `value` as a hex string such as `#12AFF0` and store it in `onValueChange`. The trigger names itself with that value.

Pass an `aria-label` that names the row, such as `Billing colour`, so the swatch is announced as `Billing colour, #12AFF0`. Also mark the first cell of each row `role="rowheader"` so a screen reader in table mode reads the row with it.
Show the effect of the choice nearby, such as a legend bar or a preview, so the colour is not judged from a 24 px circle alone.
Give the colour column a header that says what the colour is for, and centre the swatch in a narrow column.
Don't expect colours outside the six swatches. A `value` that is not in the set still shows on the trigger, but no swatch is marked and the person can only pick from the six.
Don't use it outside a table row. It is 24 px wide and has no label; use ColorPicker, which has a visible label, hex entry and opacity.
Don't use colour as the only carrier of meaning. Pair it with the name of the label or the series, as the row header does.
Don't expect the Figma Editable Cell states (Edit, Changed, Saving, Error, Disabled). CellColorPicker only has a value and a change handler.

components.title: Cell Slider
components.description: A compact progress/value slider for inline use in a Data Grid cell.

parts.name: Table
parts.description: The table the cell sits in. Its first column holds the row names and its header row names the columns. The cell control is a child of a `TableCell`.

parts.name: Column header
parts.description: The `TableHead` of the bar column. It names the measure and the unit, such as Quota used, because the bar itself carries no label.

parts.name: Row header
parts.description: The first cell of the row, marked `role="rowheader"`. It says whose level the bar shows.

parts.name: CellSlider
parts.description: A small bar with a number beside it, 112 px wide. It shows `value` out of `max` (default 100) and cannot be dragged: it is a display, not a control.

parts.name: Track
parts.description: The 4 px grey bar with fully rounded ends. It always spans the width left of the number.

parts.name: Fill
parts.description: The primary-coloured part of the track. Its width is `value / max`, capped at 100 %.

parts.name: Number
parts.description: The raw `value` to the right of the bar, 12 px and right-aligned in 28 px, so the bar never has to be read on its own.

items.text: Set `max` to the real ceiling, such as `max={5}` for a 5-point score or the seat limit of the row. The fill is clamped to the track, but the number still shows the raw value.
Put it in a column whose header names the measure and the unit, such as `Quota used`. The bar and the number carry no label or role of their own.
Mark the first cell of each row `role="rowheader"`, so the number is read with its row.
Pair it with a control when the level can change, such as a button that completes a task. The slider then follows the value.
Don't build a cell around it that is expected to be edited. It has no handler, no keyboard support and no ARIA role; use a Slider with an `aria-label` in the cell instead.
Don't use it for one task or upload with a label and a status. Progress has the role and the text for that.

Don't rely on the bar to show a value outside 0 to `max`. A value below 0, or a `max` of 0, draws an empty bar and a value above `max` a full one; the number is the only place that shows the real figure.
Don't count on the Figma Editable Cell Slider states (View, Edit, Changed, Saving, Error, Disabled): the React cell shows a level only.

components.title: Cell Select
components.description: A compact select for inline use in a Data Grid cell.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Name for screen readers — a combobox is not named by its current value.

parts.name: Table
parts.description: The table the cell sits in. Its first column holds the row names and its header row names the columns. The cell control is a child of a `TableCell`.

parts.name: Row header
parts.description: The first cell of the row, marked `role="rowheader"`. It says which row this select belongs to, so a screen reader reads it with the select.

parts.name: CellSelect
parts.description: A compact select for a table cell: a 32 px trigger, 128 px wide, with the options as a plain list of strings. It is controlled: you hold `value` and write it back in `onValueChange`.

parts.name: Trigger
parts.description: The button that shows the current value and opens the list. It is a `combobox` with no visible label, so it takes `aria-label` (default `Choose a value`).

parts.name: Value
parts.description: The current value, on one line in 12 px text. A value longer than the trigger is cut with an ellipsis.

parts.name: Chevron
parts.description: The down chevron at the right edge of the trigger. It stays inside the border at every value length.

parts.name: Options list
parts.description: The popup under the trigger, as wide as the trigger. It opens on `duration-base` and closes faster. A long option wraps onto more lines here, so the full text is always readable.

parts.name: Option
parts.description: One row of the list for each string in `options`. The highlighted option takes the page background and the chosen one shows a check.

items.text: Set `aria-label` per row and column, such as `Role of Nora Lindgren`. A trigger that shows only its value does not name itself to a screen reader.
Pass `options` as the exact strings you store and keep `value` one of them. The value is the text; there is no separate label.
Keep options short, up to about 14 characters. The trigger shows one line in 128 px and cuts the rest with an ellipsis.
Mark the first cell of each row `role="rowheader"`, so a screen reader reads the row, the column and the value together.
Don't use it for long lists or for options that need a description. It has no search and no groups; use a Combobox instead.
Don't use it in a form with a label. There the NativeSelect with its Label and helper text is the right control.
Don't pass a `value` that is not in `options`. No option is checked and the list has no starting point.
Don't expect a saving, error or disabled look. CellSelect has no such props, unlike the Editable Cell states in Figma.

components.title: Cell Switch
components.description: A compact switch for inline use in a Data Grid cell.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Name for screen readers — a cell has no visible label of its own.

parts.name: Table
parts.description: The table the cell sits in. Its first column holds the row names and its header row names the columns. The cell control is a child of a `TableCell`.

parts.name: Column header
parts.description: The `TableHead` of the switch column. It says what the switch changes, such as Email alerts. Align it the same way as the cell.

parts.name: Row header
parts.description: The first cell of the row, marked `role="rowheader"`. It says whose or which setting this is, so a screen reader reads it with the switch.

parts.name: CellSwitch
parts.description: A Switch with a default `aria-label` of `Toggle`, made for a table cell that has no visible label of its own. It is controlled: you hold `checked` and write it back in `onCheckedChange`.

parts.name: Track
parts.description: The 32 by 18 px pill. It is brand-coloured when on and grey when off, and it is the element with `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`.

parts.name: Knob
parts.description: The 16 px circle that slides from one end of the track to the other. It moves with `ease-overshoot` and swings slightly past the end.

items.text: Name every switch by its row and its column, such as `Email alerts for Nora Lindgren`. The default `Toggle` is the same in every row and tells a screen-reader user nothing.
Mark the first cell of each row `role="rowheader"` and give the switch column a header that says what it changes. The cell is then read as row, column and state.
Keep `checked` in your own state and save in the same handler that writes it back. The cell keeps no state of its own.
Align the switch like its column header: centered in a narrow column, left beside text. Use `text-center` or `text-right` on both the header and the cell.
Don't use CellSwitch outside a table. With no visible label the switch has no context; use Switch with a Label, or a Selector Item.
Don't use a switch for an action that needs a confirmation, such as deleting data. A switch applies at once.
Don't put two switches in one cell. One cell holds one value; give each value its own column.
Don't expect a saving, error or disabled look from CellSwitch. It has no such props. Use Switch with `saving` or `disabled` inside the cell when a row needs them.

components.title: Selector Item
components.description: A list row pairing a leading icon/avatar and label/description with a trailing radio, checkbox, or switch.

props.name: action
props.description: Secondary action beside the row. Rendered outside the label; clicking it never toggles the control.

props.name: announceError
props.description: Announce the error at once (`role="alert"`). Set it only for an error that appears after an action such as a failed submit; leave it off for an error that is already there when the page loads, or it is read twice.

props.name: controlPosition
props.description: Which side of the label the control sits on.

props.name: error
props.description: Error text below the row; marks the control invalid. It is linked with aria-describedby, so a screen reader reads it when the control gets focus.

props.name: helper
props.description: Hint text below the row.

props.name: layout
props.description: `card` is the bordered row; `inline` is a 24 px row without border or padding.

props.name: metadata
props.description: Short secondary text next to the control (a price, a count). Not interactive.

parts.name: SelectorItem
parts.description: The bordered row, 12 px corners. The whole row except the action is one `<label>`, so a click anywhere on it toggles the control. The border turns indigo and the fill subtle while a radio or checkbox is chosen.

parts.name: SelectorItemGroup
parts.description: A vertical stack of rows with an 8 px gap. Use it so several options read as one list.

parts.name: Leading
parts.description: An optional icon, avatar or logo before the text, passed as `leading`. The slot is at least 32 px wide and centres its content, so rows with different leading elements start their text at the same x.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: One line of 14 px medium text. It names the control for assistive technology and is cut with an ellipsis when it is too long.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: One line of secondary text under the title, 4 px below it. It describes the control for assistive technology.

parts.name: Metadata
parts.description: Short secondary text before the control, such as a price or a count. It sits inside the label and is plain text, not interactive.

parts.name: Control
parts.description: The `RadioGroupItem`, `Checkbox` or `Switch` passed as `control`. It is the one tab stop of the row and keeps its own focus ring.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: A secondary button such as Edit, passed as `action`. It sits outside the label, so a click on it never toggles the control, and it has its own tab stop.

items.text: Use SelectorItem for choices that need a title and an explanation: delivery methods, plans, a setting with a switch. For a short label next to a box, use Checkbox with a Label, and for a button-sized option use Radio Button Group.
Pass the matching control: `RadioGroupItem` inside a `RadioGroup`, or `Checkbox` or `Switch` alone. The border follows the checked state of the control, so the row needs no props for it.
Keep `title` to one line and put the detail in `description`. Both are truncated, so long text is cut with an ellipsis.
Put a secondary button in `action`, not in the title or the description. It stays outside the label and has its own tab stop.
Use `error` for a row that cannot be chosen or must be ticked. It turns the row red, marks the control invalid and links the message to it.
Don't put a link or button in `title` or `description`. The row is one label, and a click on it toggles the control.
Don't mix controls in one list, such as a switch row between radio rows. People read one control as one kind of choice.
Don't use a card row for a long list of options. Switch to the inline layout, or to a Select, once there are more than about six.

components.title: Label
components.description: An accessible label for a form control.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: A native `<label>` in a row with 8 px between its children, in 14 px medium text. Join it to a control with `htmlFor` (the `id` of the control), by putting the control inside it, or by using `FieldLabel` inside a Field. A click on it focuses the control.

parts.name: Requirement note
parts.description: A short word after the name, `Required` or `Optional`, in 12 px regular text in the tertiary colour. It is inside the label, so it is part of the accessible name and a screen reader reads it with it.

parts.name: Control
parts.description: The field the label names: an Input, a Textarea, a Checkbox. A label without a control is just text. When the control is disabled inside a Field, the label dims with it.

items.text: Use a Label for every control that has a visible name: a field above the control, a name to the left in a settings row, or the words to the right of a checkbox. Name a group of controls with a Fieldset legend, not a Label.
Join every label to its control. Inside a Field use `FieldLabel`; elsewhere give the control an `id` and the label the same `htmlFor`. The words then become a click target as large as the row.
Write the label as a short noun (`Work email`) and put a rule or an example in the helper line below the field. A label is a name, not a sentence.
Mark what is unusual. In a form where most fields are required, mark the optional ones; where most are optional, mark the required ones. Put the note inside the label, so it is read with the name.
Keep a label for a compact control and hide it with `sr-only`. A search field without a visible label still has a name and a click target for assistive technology.
Keep a button out of the label. An info tip next to a label is a sibling in the row, so a click on it does not focus the field.
Don't use a placeholder as the label. It is gone with the first keystroke and is not announced as a name on every screen reader.
Don't mark required with a colour or an asterisk alone. The word `Required` is readable by everyone; an asterisk needs an explanation on the page.
Don't leave a label unjoined. Text that looks like a label but has no `htmlFor` gives the control no name and no click target.

components.title: Field
components.description: Labelling and validation for a single form control — label, description, and error message.

props.name: actionsRef
props.description: A ref to imperative actions. - `validate`: Validates the field when called.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: dirty
props.description: Whether the field's value has been changed from its initial value. Useful when the field state is controlled by an external library.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Whether the component should ignore user interaction. Takes precedence over the `disabled` prop on the `<Field.Control>` component.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Whether the field is invalid. Useful when the field state is controlled by an external library.

props.name: name
props.description: Identifies the field when a form is submitted. Takes precedence over the `name` prop on the `<Field.Control>` component.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: touched
props.description: Whether the field has been touched. Useful when the field state is controlled by an external library.

props.name: validate
props.type: ((value: unknown, formValues: Form.Values) => string | string[] | null | void | Promise<string | string[] | null | void>)
props.description: A function for custom validation. Return a string or an array of strings with the error message(s) if the value is invalid. Returning nothing, `null`, an empty string, or an empty array means the value is valid. Asynchronous functions are…

props.name: validationDebounceTime
props.description: How long to wait between `validate` callbacks if `validationMode="onChange"` is used. Specified in milliseconds.

props.name: validationMode
props.description: Determines when the field should be validated. This takes precedence over the `validationMode` prop on `<Form>`. - `onSubmit`: triggers validation when the form is submitted, and re-validates on change after submission. - `onBlur`: trigger…

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Callback fired when the `value` changes. Use when controlled.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: match
props.description: Determines whether to show the error message according to the field's [ValidityState](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ValidityState). Specifying `true` will always show the error message, and lets external libraries contro…

props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: nativeLabel

props.name: render

aria: Connects label, description and error message to the control (aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-invalid)

parts.name: Field
parts.description: The wrapper of one control: a column with 4 px between its parts. It owns `name`, `invalid`, `disabled` and `validate`, and every part inside reads them. Its `data-invalid` and `data-disabled` attributes can be used to style the parts.

parts.name: FieldLabel
parts.description: The visible name of the control, a `<label>` in 14 px medium text with 4 px below it. It is linked to the control, so a click on it focuses the control, and it is the accessible name. It dims with a disabled field.

parts.name: Control
parts.description: The control itself. An `Input` joins the Field by itself; any other control, such as a Textarea, joins through `FieldControl` and its `render` prop. The control receives `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` from the Field.

parts.name: FieldDescription
parts.description: The hint under the control in 12 px tertiary text. It is linked with `aria-describedby`, so a screen reader reads it after the label. It dims with a disabled field.

parts.name: FieldError
parts.description: The error message in 12 px error text. It renders only while the field is invalid (or when `match` is set), is linked with `aria-describedby` and is left out while the field is disabled. Hide the hint while it shows, so the two never stand together.

items.text: Use Field around every control that has a label, a hint or an error. It does not draw a box: the control keeps its own border. For a group of related controls, put the Fields in a Fieldset; to send a form and take errors from a server, use Form.
Put a `FieldLabel` first, then the control, then the `FieldDescription` or the `FieldError`. A label is a noun (`Work email`) and a hint is a full sentence.
Give each Field a `name` when it sits in a Form. The name is how an error that you pass to the Form's `errors` finds its field.
Write the error as an instruction: `Enter an email address like name@company.com`, not `Invalid`. Show it after the person leaves the field or sends the form, and keep what they typed.
Render the hint only while there is no error, so the error takes its place and the two never stand together. Keep a line of room for the message, so the controls below do not jump.
Mark an exception on the label row (`Optional`), not in the placeholder. A placeholder is gone once the person starts to type.
Don't build the label, hint and error by hand with `
Don't put two controls in one Field. The label names one control; two controls need a Fieldset with a legend.
Don't set `disabled` on the control and leave the Field enabled. The label and the hint then stay at full strength next to a dimmed control.

parts.name: Fieldset
parts.description: The group: a native `<fieldset>`, so it has the group role. By default it is a card with a 1 px border, a 12 px corner, 16 px of padding and 20 px between its children. Its `aria-labelledby` points to the legend, which is the accessible name of the group.

parts.name: FieldsetLegend
parts.description: The name of the group in 14 px semibold text. It is a `<div>` linked to the fieldset with an id, so it can sit anywhere inside it, on a row with a note. It dims with a disabled fieldset.

parts.name: Hint
parts.description: A line under the legend in 12 px tertiary text that states the rule. Give it an id and point to it with `aria-describedby` on the fieldset, so a screen reader reads it with the group.

parts.name: Controls
parts.description: The related controls: checkbox rows, a radio group or fields. Keep 12 px between rows of one kind and 16 px between columns.

parts.name: Legend note
parts.description: A word such as Required beside the legend, in 12 px tertiary text. It is for sighted readers; put the rule itself in the hint so a screen reader hears it.

parts.name: Group error
parts.description: One message under the controls that says what to do, with a 14 px alert icon. Give it an id and join it with `aria-describedby`. A fieldset has no invalid prop: set `data-invalid` and the card takes the red border and tint.

items.text: Use a Fieldset when several controls answer one question: a set of checkboxes, the radios of one choice, the fields of an address. One control with its own label needs a Field, not a Fieldset.
Write the legend as the question or the noun of the group (`Notification channels`, `Shipping address`). It is read before every control in the group, so keep it short.
State the rule in a hint under the legend and join it with `aria-describedby`. Say it before the person breaks it: `Choose where we send alerts`.
Show one error for the group, not one per control, and say what to do: `Select at least one option to continue`. Show it after the first try to continue, and keep what was chosen.
Use the plain surface (`border-0 bg-transparent p-0`) when the group sits straight on the page, and the card when the group must stand apart, such as an address block in a long form.
To switch a group off, set `disabled` on the Fieldset. For a checkbox or a radio group, also pass `disabled` to the control, or wrap each in a Field, because only Fields read the Fieldset.
Don't use a Fieldset to draw a box around unrelated content. It names a group for assistive technology; use a Card for a visual container.
Don't nest a Fieldset in a Fieldset to indent. Nest only when the inner group has a name of its own.
Don't leave the legend out and put the question in a heading next to the group. The group then has no name for a screen reader.

parts.name: Form
parts.description: The `<form>` element in a vertical stack with 20 px between its children. It turns the browser's own validation bubbles off, calls `onFormSubmit` with the values of the named fields when every field is valid, and focuses the first invalid field when one is not.

parts.name: Error summary
parts.description: An `Alert` with `variant="negative"` above the fields: a title with the count, and one line per field that moves focus to it. It is yours to add; use it when a form is long enough that an error can be out of sight. It is an alert, so a screen reader announces it when it appears.

parts.name: Field
parts.description: One labelled control with its helper and error line. The `name` joins it to the values that `onFormSubmit` receives and to the messages in `errors`. Its `FieldError` shows under the control when the field is invalid and the helper line stays.

parts.name: Status line
parts.description: One line of 12 px text above the actions that says what the form is doing: checking, saving, saved or unsaved. It is a polite live region, so the change is announced without taking focus.

parts.name: Form actions
parts.description: The row of buttons at the end, built with `FormActions`. The button with `type="submit"` sends the form, and so does Enter in a text field.

items.text: Use a Form for everything a person sends together. A single field that acts at once, such as a search box, needs no Form. A setting that takes effect at once is a Switch.

Give every Field a `name` and handle the send in `onFormSubmit`. It receives the values by name and is only called when every field is valid, so Enter in a field and the Save button take the same path.
Say what to do in the message: `Enter a work email address, like name@company.com`, not `Invalid input`. Show it under the field, keep what the person typed and keep the helper line.
Move focus to the first invalid field after a failed send, and add an error summary when the form is long. The summary lists each field and jumps to it; it never replaces the message at the field.

Show the work: a pending Save button with its own label (`Saving…`), the way out disabled while it runs, and a confirmation when it is done. Say `All changes saved` in the status line, not only with a colour.

Keep the default `validationMode` (`onSubmit`) for most forms: the first check waits for the first Save, and the field then re-checks as the person corrects it. Use `onBlur` for a field that is expensive to get wrong, such as an address.

Don't disable the submit button to signal an invalid form. A disabled button gives no reason; let the person press it and tell them what is wrong. Disable it only when there is nothing to send, such as a settings form without changes.
Don't clear the fields after an error, and don't clear them after a server failure. Name the problem, keep the entries and offer Try again.
Don't add an `onClick` to the submit button to run the check. Use `onFormSubmit`, so a keyboard user and a mouse user take the same path.

components.title: Input Group
components.description: Groups an input with leading/trailing addons — icons, buttons, or text.

parts.name: InputGroup
parts.description: The bordered frame: 1 px border, 8 px corner, white fill, 8 px between its children and 12 px of side padding. It owns the height (`--field-md`, 36 px), the hover border, the focus ring and the red border for an invalid input. The input inside it loses its own border and ring.

parts.name: Leading content
parts.description: An icon or a short text before the value, in an `InputGroupAddon`: a search icon, a mail icon, `https://`. It is not interactive, sits in the tertiary text colour and keeps icons at 16 px.

parts.name: Input
parts.description: The field itself, a plain `Input` or any native `<input>` as a direct child. It fills the space that is left, with no border, fill or padding of its own. Its `aria-invalid` and `disabled` are read by the frame.

parts.name: Trailing content
parts.description: A unit, a shortcut or a button after the value: `USD`, a key hint, show or hide, clear, copy. A button here is a 32 px `IconButton` that sits 2 px inside the frame with a 6 px corner, concentric with the 8 px corner of the group.

items.text: Use an Input Group when something belongs inside the field's border: an icon that says what the field is, a fixed part of the value, or a small action on the value. An action that is not about the value is a button beside the field.
Put the `<input>` as a direct child of the group. The group styles `> input` and cannot reach an input that is wrapped in another element.

Keep the corners concentric. A 32 px `IconButton` in a 36 px group sits 2 px inside the 1 px border, so give it a 6 px corner (`rounded-[calc(var(--radius-md)-0.125rem)]`) and the group `pr-px` (or `px-px` for a button on each side).
Name the button with `aria-label` and tell the state with `aria-pressed` for a toggle such as show or hide. An icon alone is not a name.
Set `aria-invalid` and `disabled` on the input, not on the group. The group reads them with `:has()` and turns the border red or dims itself.
Give the group a height class for the other sizes: `h-(--field-sm)` or `h-(--field-lg)`. The inner button stays 32 px, so use it in the default and large sizes.
Don't put the main action of a form inside the field. Apply, Send and Subscribe are buttons of their own, next to the field.
Don't put a second field or a long text in an addon. An addon is a unit, an icon or a short word.
Don't rely on the addon text for the name of the field. `https://` is part of the value; the field still needs a Label.

Shift + Arrow: largeStep (default 10)
Alt + Arrow: smallStep (default 0.1)

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The visible name of the field, a `Label` with `htmlFor` that matches the `id` of the `NumberField`. A click on it focuses the input. A field that has no room for a label takes an `aria-label` on the input instead.

parts.name: NumberField
parts.description: The root. It holds the number (`null` when the field is empty), the limits, the steps and the `format`, and it has no element of its own. Its `id` goes on the input.

parts.name: NumberFieldGroup
parts.description: The bordered frame around the buttons and the input: 36 px high with an 8 px corner and 1 px dividers between the parts. It carries the hover border, the indigo focus ring and the red error state.

parts.name: NumberFieldDecrement
parts.description: The minus button on the left, 36 px wide. It lowers the value by `step` and dims and stops at `min`. Its default name is `Decrease`; name it after what it changes.

parts.name: NumberFieldInput
parts.description: The text input, 64 px wide by default with the number centred. It takes only characters that can be part of a number, formats the value on blur and answers the arrow keys, Home and End.

parts.name: NumberFieldIncrement
parts.description: The plus button on the right, 36 px wide. It raises the value by `step` and dims and stops at `max`. Its default name is `Increase`.

items.text: Give the field a visible label and join it with `htmlFor` and the `id` of `NumberField`. Where a column header already names it, put an `aria-label` on `NumberFieldInput`.
Set `min`, `max` and `step` to the real limits, such as `min={1} max={50}`. The buttons stop at the edges and Home and End jump to them.
Name the buttons after what they change, such as `Add a seat` and `Remove a seat`. The default `Increase` and `Decrease` do not say what grows.

Put the unit in `format` (`{ style: "unit", unit: "kilogram" }`) or in the label, so the number is never read without it. Widen the input with `className="w-24"` when the formatted text is longer than 64 px.
Treat the value as `number | null`. A field the person emptied reports `null`, not `0`; show an error under it and mark the input `aria-invalid`.
Don't use it for a number nobody types or steps in small amounts, such as a year or a phone number. Use an Input with the right `inputMode`.
Don't use it for a count of one to ten where there is no typing. Number Stepper is a smaller control for that.
Don't leave the input without a name. The buttons have names; the input has none unless you give it a label or an `aria-label`.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The visible name of the code, a `Label` with `htmlFor` that matches the `id` of the `OtpField`. It names the group and the first slot. A click on it focuses the field.

parts.name: OtpField
parts.description: The group of slots: a `<div role="group">` that holds the value as one string, fills and clears the slots, moves focus and fires `onValueComplete` when the last slot is filled. `length` is required and must match the number of slots. It also renders a hidden input, so the code is submitted with the form under `name`.

parts.description: One slot for one character: a native `<input>` 40 px square with an 8 px corner and a 1 px border. Render one per character. Only one slot at a time is in the tab order. Give every slot after the first an `aria-label` such as `Digit 2 of 6`; the first slot takes its name from the label.

parts.name: Message
parts.description: The line under the slots in 12 px type, 4 px below them: a `FieldDescription` with the rule, a `FieldError` with what to do, or a status with an icon for an expired, pending or verified code. An error replaces the helper; it never stands next to it.

items.text: Use an OTP Field for a short code that is typed once: an email or SMS code, an authenticator code, a PIN. A code with dashes, letters of any length or a recovery key is a text field, so use an Input.
Render one `OtpFieldInput` per character and set the same number in `length`. A code of six digits needs six slots.

Give the field a visible `Label` with `htmlFor` that matches the `id`, and name every slot after the first with `aria-label` (`Digit 2 of 6`). A screen reader then announces the position, not just `edit text`.
Leave `autoComplete` at its default `one-time-code`, so a phone offers the code from the message. The first slot takes the paste; the field spreads it across the slots.
Check the code in `onValueComplete`, or set `autoSubmit` inside a form. The person should not have to find a button after the last digit.
Say what to do when a code fails: `That code is not correct. Check it and try again.` or `This code has expired.` with a Resend action. Keep what was typed so a wrong digit can be fixed.
Don't change `length` while the person is typing, and don't put codes of different lengths in one field. Render another field instead.
Don't use an OTP Field for a long or free-form value. A long code is hard to check by eye in slots; use an Input.
Don't use real or reused codes in examples, tests or screenshots. Use demo values such as 470921.

parts.name: Combobox
parts.description: The root. It holds the chosen value, the typed text, the items and the filter, and renders nothing itself. `value` is an entry of `items`, or `null`; with `multiple` it is an array.

parts.name: ComboboxInputGroup
parts.description: The bordered frame around the input and the chevron, 36 px high with an 8 px corner. It draws the border and the focus ring, dims when the field is disabled and turns red when the input is invalid.

parts.name: ComboboxInput
parts.description: The text input. It is a combobox: typing filters the list, the arrow keys move through it, Enter chooses an entry and Escape closes the list. Give it a visible label or an `aria-label`.

parts.name: ComboboxTrigger
parts.description: The chevron button that opens and closes the whole list. It is named `Show options` and is not in the tab order, because the keyboard opens the list from the input.

parts.name: ComboboxPopup
parts.description: The list panel. It brings its own portal and positioner, matches the width of the field and scrolls when it runs out of room. Its 12 px corner is concentric with the 8 px rows inside its 4 px padding.

parts.name: ComboboxList
parts.description: Renders the entries. Pass a render function as the child, so the filtered list, not the full one, is mapped. With groups it receives one group at a time.

parts.name: ComboboxGroup
parts.description: Holds the entries of one group under a `ComboboxGroupLabel`. A group without a match disappears with its label.

parts.name: ComboboxGroupLabel
parts.description: The heading of a group, 12 px medium text in the muted colour. It is not an entry, so arrow keys skip it.

parts.name: ComboboxItem
parts.description: One entry, 32 px high for a single line. Its `value` is what the field holds when it is chosen. A row can hold an icon, or an avatar and a second line. The highlighted row takes the `bg-page` fill.

parts.name: Check
parts.description: A 16 px check at the right of the chosen entry. With `multiple` every chosen entry shows one.

parts.name: ComboboxEmpty
parts.description: A centred line shown in place of the list when nothing matches. It is hidden while it has no content.

parts.name: ComboboxPortal
parts.description: Moves the list to the end of the document. `ComboboxPopup` already renders it; you only need it for a custom `container`.

items.text: Give the input a visible label with `Label` and `htmlFor`. The placeholder is a hint such as `Search projects`, not the name of the field.
Always include a `ComboboxEmpty` with a sentence such as `No projects match.` so a list without matches never looks broken.
Keep the state as `useState<Value | null>`. The value is `null` while nothing is chosen and after the choice is cleared.
With `multiple`, show the chosen entries next to the field, as a count or a list. The field only shows what people type.
Group a long list by what people already know, such as an area or a team, and pass the groups as `items`.
Don't use it for free text. Text that is not an entry is dropped when the field loses focus; use an Autocomplete when any value is valid.
Don't use it for a short list people can see at a glance. A Native Select is quicker when there are about a dozen options or fewer.
Don't turn on `multiple` and then hide the choices. People cannot tell what is selected from a closed field with a placeholder.

parts.description: The root. It holds the text of the field, the items and the filter, and renders nothing itself. `value` is the text in the input, not a chosen item.

parts.description: The text input. It is a combobox: typing filters the suggestions, the arrow keys move through them, Enter takes one and Escape closes the list. Give it a visible label or an `aria-label`.

parts.name: AutocompletePopup
parts.description: The suggestion panel. It brings its own portal and positioner, matches the width of the field and scrolls when it runs out of room. Its 12 px corner is concentric with the 8 px rows inside its 4 px padding.

parts.name: AutocompleteList
parts.description: Renders the items. Pass a render function as the child, `(item) => <AutocompleteItem ... />`, so the filtered list, not the full one, is mapped.

parts.name: AutocompleteItem
parts.description: One suggestion, 32 px high for a single line. Its `value` is what fills the field when it is chosen. A row can hold an icon, or an avatar and a second line. The highlighted row takes the `bg-page` fill.

parts.name: AutocompleteEmpty
parts.description: A centred line shown in place of the list when nothing matches. It is hidden while it has no content.
