items.text: Give the input a visible label with `Label` and `htmlFor`. The placeholder is a hint such as `Search cities`, not the name of the field.
Always include an `AutocompleteEmpty` with a sentence such as `No cities match.` so a list without matches never looks broken.
Control `value` with state when the text drives something else, such as a search on the server. The value is the text of the field, never an item object.
Keep the suggestions few, five to eight, and one line each. Use `limit` to cap a long list; people pick by reading, so a row with several lines or controls slows them down.
Don't treat the value as validated. Text that matches no suggestion still ends up in `value`, so check it on submit or use a Combobox.
Don't use it for a choice that must come from the list. A Combobox keeps the field on a value of the list and tells people when nothing matches.
Don't use it as a menu of actions. Suggestions fill a field; actions belong in a Dropdown Menu.

components.title: Calendar
components.description: A month grid for picking one date or a range, with keyboard navigation and optional min, max and disabled days.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Days inside min–max that cannot be picked. They stay reachable with the arrow keys and are announced as unavailable.

props.name: disabledReason
props.description: When set, every blocked day is wrapped in a Tooltip with this text.

props.name: header
props.description: Header style: a plain label or clickable month/year buttons.

props.name: hoverDay
props.description: Shows the range preview up to this day as if it were hovered.

props.name: markedDays
props.description: Days that get a dot under the number.

props.name: markedLabel
props.description: Label appended to marked days' aria-label.

props.name: max
props.description: Latest day that can be picked. Keyboard focus stops here and later months cannot be opened.

props.name: min
props.description: Earliest day that can be picked. Keyboard focus stops here and earlier months cannot be opened.

props.name: navigation
props.description: Which navigation arrows to show. Hidden arrows keep their slot.

props.name: reasonDefaultOpenDay
props.description: The day whose disabled tooltip starts open (for documentation).

props.name: size
props.description: The size of the day cells.

props.name: status
props.description: Status of the calendar data. Anything but "ready" prevents picking.

props.name: today
props.description: Overrides "today" (default `new Date()`).

keyboard: Tab: into the day grid once (selected day, today or the first day) and to the month buttons
Arrow keys: previous / next day and week; Home / End: start / end of the week
Page Up / Page Down: previous / next month (Shift: year), the same day clamped to the month
Enter / Space: choose the focused day
aria: role=grid labelled by the month name (aria-live), rows, weekday columnheaders and gridcells
The chosen day's cell aria-selected; today aria-current="date"; days outside min / max or in disabled are aria-disabled and cannot be chosen
Previous / Next month buttons are labelled and disabled when the month lies outside min / max

parts.name: Calendar
parts.description: An inline month grid, Monday first, in `single` or `range` mode. It has two sizes: `sm` with 32 px days (224 px wide, the default) and `md` with 40 px days (280 px wide). It has no popover and no field, so place it in a card, or use DatePicker for a field. `min`, `max` and `disabled` limit which days can be picked.

parts.name: CalendarHeader
parts.description: The month title between the previous and next buttons. `header="label"` shows a title such as `November 2026`; `header="month-year"` shows two buttons that open the month and year picker. `navigation` shows both arrows, one or none, and a hidden arrow keeps its slot so the title stays centred. A button is disabled when its whole month lies outside `min` and `max`.

parts.name: Weekday labels
parts.description: A row of seven `columnheader` cells, Mo to Su, each named with the full weekday for screen readers. The grid always shows six weeks, so its height never changes with the month.

parts.name: CalendarDay
parts.description: One `<button>` per day in a `gridcell`. What a day means is separate from how the pointer touches it: selection (`single`, `start`, `middle`, `end`, `preview`), today, outside the month and unavailable describe the date; hover, pressed and focus describe the pointer. The chosen day's cell has `aria-selected` and today has `aria-current="date"`. The figure marks the start of a range.

parts.name: Range band
parts.description: In `mode="range"` the days between the start and the end are squared tint cells that touch, so the band reads as one shape, and the start and end are filled with rounded outer ends. While only the start exists, hovering a later day previews the band up to it.

parts.name: Marked day
parts.description: `markedDays` puts a dot under the number of a day that has data, such as an event or an open slot. The dot is never the only cue: `markedLabel` is added to the day's accessible name.

parts.name: Today
parts.description: Today has a ring on top of any selection. `today` overrides the date of today, which is useful for demos and tests.

parts.name: CalendarPeriodPicker
parts.description: A 3 by 4 grid of months (`type="month"`) or of twelve years (`type="year"`) with its own previous and next buttons. The current period has a ring, the selection is filled, and periods outside `min` and `max` are unavailable. It opens from the month and year header and also works on its own. Its cells are `CalendarPeriodCell` buttons.

parts.name: Restriction
parts.description: `disabledReason` shows why a day is blocked, in a tooltip and in the day's accessible name. `status` (`loading`, `empty` or `error`) blocks every day while data loads or fails; the banner that explains it is composed next to the calendar.

items.text: Use Calendar to show a month inline, next to a schedule or inside your own popover. To pick a date into a form field, use DatePicker, which puts a Calendar in a popover.

Set `mode="range"` and keep `selected` as `{ from, to }`. The first click sets `from`, the second sets `to` (an earlier day swaps the two) and a third click starts a new range. A range without `to` is a draft, so say in the interface what is missing.
Use `size="md"` (40 px days) when the calendar is the main control and `sm` (32 px) in dense panels.

Use `header="month-year"` for birth dates and other far dates, so nobody pages month by month. Open on the right month with `defaultMonth`, or control `month` and `onMonthChange` when two calendars must move together.
Limit the choice with `min` and `max`, and block single days with `disabled` (a list of dates or a test such as weekends). Give the reason with `disabledReason` or in the text near the calendar.
Mark days that carry data with `markedDays` and name the meaning with `markedLabel`, for example `has events` or `has open slots`.
While data loads or fails, set `status` and show a banner beside the calendar that says why the days are blocked, with a way to retry.
Don't use a dot as the only way to learn that a day has events. Keep `markedLabel` meaningful and list the events next to the calendar.
Don't show hover, pressed or the range preview as a confirmed choice. A confirmed day never changes on hover, and a preview band is lighter than the chosen range.
Don't block days without saying why. A blocked day is announced as unavailable, but a sighted person sees only a dimmed number.

components.title: Date Picker
components.description: A Calendar inside a Popover, with Cancel/Apply actions.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Days that cannot be picked: a list of dates or a test (passed to Calendar).

props.name: max
props.description: Latest day that can be picked (passed to Calendar).

props.name: min
props.description: Earliest day that can be picked (passed to Calendar).

props.name: numberOfMonths
props.description: Months shown side by side. Defaults to 2 for range mode.

props.name: presets
props.description: Quick-select sidebar (Figma: Type=presets). `true` uses the built-in presets.

keyboard: Enter / Space on the trigger: open the calendar
In the calendar: the Calendar date-grid keys (arrows, Home / End, Page Up / Page Down, Enter)
Esc: close
aria: Give the trigger an accessible name (aria-label or a Field label)
min, max and disabled reach the Calendar: blocked days are aria-disabled

parts.name: DatePicker
parts.description: The trigger and the popover in one component. `appearance="button"` (the default) is a plain button with a calendar icon and the value; `appearance="field"` is a field with a label, a format hint and an error line. `mode` is `single` or `range`. It is controlled with `value` and `onValueChange`, and `open` and `onOpenChange` control the popover.

parts.name: Trigger
parts.description: The element that opens the popover: a button, a field, or with `typeable` a text field with the calendar icon in front of the text, which is the button that opens the calendar. It shows `Pick a date` or the format hint while empty, and the chosen date or range after. `fieldState` makes it `disabled` (does not open) or `readonly` (focusable, does not open).

parts.name: DatePickerPanel
parts.description: The content of the popover: the calendars, the presets and the footer, 16 px from the edge. It also works on its own on the page: set `surface` to give it a border and a surface. A range shows two months side by side, and a single date one. The popover is as wide as its content (312 px for one month).

parts.name: Presets
parts.description: `presets` adds a column of quick ranges at the left, such as `Last 7 days`. `true` uses eight built-in ones; an array of `{ label, range }` uses your own. Choosing one fills the draft, and Apply still confirms. A preset that lies completely outside `min` and `max` is disabled.

parts.name: Calendar
parts.description: A medium Calendar with its own header and arrows: two for a range (the first has the previous arrow, the last the next) and one for a single date. `min`, `max` and `disabled` go straight to it. See the Calendar page for its keys and states.

parts.name: Summary
parts.description: The line at the left of the footer. It says what is missing (`Nov 22, 2026 – select an end date`), explains an error, or shows the choice, for a range with its length in days or nights (`unit`).

parts.name: Cancel and Apply
parts.description: Cancel closes the popover and drops the draft. Apply commits the draft and closes it, and is disabled while there is nothing valid to commit. With `confirmation="instant"` the footer is left out.

parts.name: DatePickerField
parts.description: The closed field alone, without a popover, with its label and helper line. It is what `DatePicker` draws for `appearance="field"` and is useful to show the field next to an inline panel.

parts.name: DatePickerFooter
parts.description: The summary line with Cancel and Apply, as its own part, for panels you compose yourself.

items.text: Use the default button for a filter in a toolbar, and `appearance="field"` in a form, where it needs a label, a hint and an error line.
Use `typeable` for dates far in the past or future, such as a date of birth. Typing is faster than paging, and the field takes `MM/DD/YYYY` or a written date such as `Nov 12, 2026`.
Use `mode="range"` with `presets` for reporting, where people usually want Last 7 days or Month to date. Keep `numberOfMonths` at its default; the picker shows one month below 830 px on its own.
Use `confirmation="instant"` for a single date that is easy to change, such as a due date. Keep Apply and Cancel for ranges and for dates that trigger work, such as a booking.
Limit the choice with `min`, `max` and `disabled`. They block days in the calendar and are enforced when a date is typed.
Say what an unfinished or invalid range needs. The field shows `Select an end date to finish the range.` or the error, and Apply stays off until the range is valid.
Don't use `confirmation="instant"` with `mode="range"`: without the footer a range has nothing to commit it.
Don't use a Date Picker for a month on a schedule next to your content. Use Calendar, which has no popover.
Don't leave the label out of a field. The format hint disappears once a date is chosen, but the label stays.

components.title: Alert
components.description: An inline banner in 5 colors and 2 sizes, with an optional close button and action.

props.name: icon
props.description: Replaces the leading icon (default: a check circle, a warning triangle for negative and warning). `null` hides it.

aria: Has role="alert", so a screen reader announces it when it appears on the page. A message that is already there on load is not read out; for a short confirmation after an action use a toast

parts.name: Alert
parts.description: The banner. It renders a `div` with `role="alert"`, takes a `variant` of `plain`, `positive`, `primary`, `negative` or `warning` and a `size` of `large` or `small`, and picks its icon from the variant.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The leading icon: a check circle, or a warning triangle for `negative` and `warning`. Replace it with `icon`, hide it with `icon={null}`.

parts.name: AlertTitle
parts.description: The bold first line. In the `small` size it stays on one line and only truncates when the banner is very narrow.

parts.name: AlertDescription
parts.description: The message. In `large` it wraps under the title; in `small` it takes the rest of the line and ends in an ellipsis.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A native button named Dismiss that calls `onClose`. It is only drawn when `onClose` is set.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: Any `Button` placed after the description, usually `plain` and `sm`. In `large` it sits under the text; in `small` it ends the row.

items.text: Say what happened in the title and what to do next in the text, for example `Changes couldn't be saved` and `Check your connection and try again.`
Pick the colour for the meaning: `positive` for done, `negative` for failed, `warning` for attention, `primary` for information and `plain` for a neutral note.
Place the alert next to what it is about: under the field that failed, or at the top of the section it describes.
Give an alert that is only information a close button with `onClose`, and keep one that blocks people on the page until the cause is fixed.
Don't use an alert for a confirmation that should vanish by itself. A Toast fits a short message after an action.
Don't stack more than two or three alerts. Merge them into one, or move the details into a list.
Don't rely on the colour alone. The title and the text must say what happened, because not everyone sees the colour.
Don't put long text or a form in an alert. Link to a page for the details.

components.title: Toast
components.description: A temporary notification that appears in the corner of the screen, with success/error/warning/info types.

props.name: position
props.description: Corner the stack lives in.

props.name: limit
props.description: The maximum number of toasts that can be displayed at once. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest toasts are marked as `limited` (via the `data-limited` attribute) rather than removed, so they can be hidden or animated out.

props.name: timeout
props.description: The default amount of time (in ms) before a toast is auto dismissed. A value of `0` will prevent the toast from being dismissed automatically.

props.name: toastManager
props.description: A global manager for toasts to use outside of a React component.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

keyboard: Toasts do not take focus; the close button is reachable with Tab
aria: Announced to screen readers through the Base UI toast live region
The close button is labelled "Close"

parts.name: Toaster
parts.description: The one-line setup. It wraps your app in a provider, renders the viewport and draws every toast. `position` picks the corner: `top-right` or `bottom-right`.

parts.name: ToastProvider
parts.description: The provider on its own, with a default `timeout` of 5000 ms and a `limit` of 3 toasts in the stack. Toaster already includes it.

parts.name: ToastViewport
parts.description: The fixed region in the corner, a live region labelled Notifications that holds the stack. Toaster already renders it.

parts.name: Toast
parts.description: One notification, a card with a border and a shadow. Older toasts sit smaller and fainter behind the newest; hovering or focusing the stack spreads them into a list.

parts.name: Type dot
parts.description: The small dot that shows the `type`: green for `success`, red for `error`, yellow for `warning` and indigo for `info`.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The bold first line that names the outcome, such as `Settings saved`.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: One line of detail under the title. It is only drawn when the toast has a `description`.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: A text button in the link colour, such as Undo. It is only drawn when the toast has `actionProps`, which take the label as `children` and an `onClick`.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A button named Close that closes the toast at once.

items.text: Write the title as the outcome in a few words, such as `Settings saved`, and use the description only for detail people need, such as what to do next.
Offer Undo through `actionProps` for actions that people can take back, such as a delete, instead of asking them to confirm first.
Use `toast.promise` for work that takes a while, so one toast goes from loading to success or error.
Add the Toaster once, high in the app, and call `useToast()` only below it.
Don't use a toast for a problem people have to fix. It goes away; keep an Alert on the page until the cause is gone.
Don't put information in a toast that is nowhere else. It can be missed or closed, so the result must also show on the page.
Don't fire several toasts for one action. Merge them into one message; the stack shows three at a time.
Don't make many toasts stay with `timeout: 0`. Keep that for a warning people must act on.

components.title: Pull to Refresh
components.description: Drag down from the top of any content past a threshold to trigger an async refresh, with a rotating spinner and a rubber-band release.

props.name: onError
props.description: Called when `onRefresh` throws or its promise rejects. The indicator resets either way and the rejection is not left unhandled; without `onError` the failure is swallowed here, so show it in your own UI.

parts.name: PullToRefresh
parts.description: A `relative overflow-hidden` box around your content. Give it a height where the list should not grow, and a background: the indicator sits behind the content, and the box shows it as the content moves down. The pull starts only when everything above is scrolled to the top.

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The spinner icon at the top of the box, as high as `threshold`. It fades in and turns with the pull, then spins until `onRefresh` settles. It is `pointer-events-none` and hidden from the pointer.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The wrapper around `children` that moves down with the pull. It takes the pointer events, sets `touch-action` so the browser keeps scrolling the content up, and uses a grab cursor. Text inside it cannot be selected.

items.text: Return the promise from `onRefresh`. The spinner and the lock stay until it settles, so a slow request never looks finished.

Pass `onError` and show the failure in text, such as `Couldn't refresh`. The component resets after a rejection or a throw and does not show anything itself; without `onError` the failure is swallowed silently, with no unhandled rejection.
Put a visible Refresh button beside the list that calls the same function. The gesture is pointer-based and has no keyboard route and no announcement.
Announce the result in text with `role="status"`, such as `Updated just now`. The component says nothing to assistive technology.
Give the box a height, a background and content that fills it. The box clips what moves out of it, and its background is what shows behind the content during the pull.
Keep `threshold` at or below `maxPull` (defaults 70 and 110). The pull moves at half the finger speed, so people drag about twice the threshold.
Don't make the gesture the only way to refresh. Many people use a keyboard, a switch or a screen reader, and on a desktop mouse the drag is easy to miss.
Don't use it for data that updates by itself. Show the new state instead and skip the gesture.
Don't put text people should select inside the content. The content has `select-none` so a drag does not select text, which means it cannot be copied from there.
Don't expect a tap to work right after a pull. The click that ends a drag is swallowed on purpose, so the item under the finger is not opened.

components.title: Rating
components.description: An interactive star rating input.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group ("Rating" by default); read-only, it replaces "Rated 3.5 out of 5".

props.name: aria-labelledby
props.description: Id of a visible label that names the group, instead of `aria-label`.

keyboard: Arrow Left / Right: change the rating
aria: Interactive: role=radiogroup with one role=radio per star; read-only: role=img with a label

parts.name: Rating
parts.description: The group of options. Interactive it is a `radiogroup` with one Tab stop; with `readOnly` it is a single image that reads `Rated 3.5 out of 5`. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

parts.name: Option
parts.description: One radio of the group: a star or a heart (24 px with a 16 px icon), a face (48 px) or a number of the scale (40 px high). Hover previews the fill of stars and hearts; a click or an arrow key chooses.

parts.name: Filled icon
parts.description: A star in the yellow brand tone or a heart in the pink one, filled up to the value.

parts.name: Empty icon
parts.description: The outline in the control border colour for the options beyond the value.

parts.name: Value label
parts.description: The number beside the row, with `label="left"` or `label="right"`. With `label="tooltip"` a dark bubble with an arrow shows it above the chosen option instead.

parts.name: RatingCell
parts.description: A read-only star row with the value on the right, made for table cells. Takes `value` and `max`.

items.text: Pick the type for the question: `stars` for an opinion, `hearts` for favorites, `emojis` for a mood, `scale` for a 0 to 10 survey answer such as Net Promoter Score.
Give every interactive Rating a visible question and tie it with `aria-labelledby`, or set `aria-label`. The default name is only Rating. Keep one Rating per question.
Set `readOnly` when you display an average. A fractional `value` such as 3.5 fills the nearest icon and keeps the exact number in the accessible name.
Turn on `label="right"` when the number matters. Without it, a score of 4.5 is only a row of icons.
Show a comment field after a low score, so people can say what went wrong. Send the score only when they confirm it.
Don't put `label="tooltip"` against the top edge of a container. The bubble floats about 32 px above the row and takes no space in the layout, so leave room for it.
Don't expect hover to choose. It previews the fill of stars and hearts, but only a click or an arrow key calls `onValueChange`; arrows move and choose in one step.
Don't use the `emojis` type for a required answer. Clicking the chosen face again clears it and sends `0`.

components.title: Trend Chip
components.description: A small pill showing a change, up or down, in seven icon styles.

props.name: direction
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Trend; `flat` is the old name for `neutral`.

props.name: icon
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Icon; the same glyph turns for `down`.

props.name: sentiment
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Sentiment: whether the change is good or bad. `auto` colours by direction (up green, down red); use `positive` for a fall that is good (churn, cost) or `negative` for a rise that is bad. The arrow always follows `directi…

parts.name: TrendChip
parts.description: An inline `<span>` with a glyph and a label. It is not interactive and holds no state: you pass the finished label, the direction and, where the colour should not follow the direction, the sentiment.

parts.name: Pill
parts.description: The rounded surface, 20 px high. Its colour comes from the sentiment: a green tint for positive, a red tint for negative and a grey one for neutral. It also carries `data-direction` and `data-sentiment`.

parts.name: Glyph
parts.description: One of seven icons chosen with `icon`. The same glyph turns for `down`. A neutral chip always shows a minus. The glyph follows the text colour and is hidden from screen readers.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The `value` string at 12 px, semibold. It is the only part a screen reader reads, so it carries the sign and the unit.

parts.name: TrendCaret
parts.description: The filled triangle behind the `triangle` icon, also used by the change label of Number Value. It is exported on its own for your own layouts. It is decorative and `aria-hidden`.

items.text: Write the sign and the unit into `value`: `+12.4%`, `-3 pts`, `+$1,204`. The glyph is hidden from screen readers, so the label is all they get.

Keep direction and meaning apart. `direction` sets which way the glyph points and `sentiment` sets the colour: a falling churn rate is `direction="down"` with `sentiment="positive"`, a rising ticket count is `direction="up"` with `sentiment="negative"`.
Choose one `icon` style per screen and keep it. The padding follows the glyph, so mixed styles in a column do not line up.
Name what the change is measured against, in the chip (`+4.2% vs last month`) or in the text beside it. A change without a reference says little.
Don't leave `sentiment` on `auto` for a metric where a fall is good. `auto` colours by direction, so a falling error rate would show red.
Don't rely on colour alone. Green and red do not reach everyone, so the sign in the label and the direction of the glyph say the same thing.
Don't use it for a status or a count. A chip shows a change; for a state such as Paid or Failed use Badge.
Don't use `direction="flat"` in new code. It is the old name for `neutral`.

components.title: Pressable Feedback
components.description: Wraps any content with a scale-down press animation.

props.name: asChild
props.description: Apply the press effect to the child element instead of wrapping it.

parts.name: PressableFeedback
parts.description: Scales its content down to 95 % at 90 % opacity while it is pressed. Alone it renders a `<button type="button">` around `children`; with `asChild` it lends the effect to its single child. It brings the focus ring and nothing else: the look is yours.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: What you pass as `children`: a label, an icon with a label, a card body. It scales together with the button, so keep it inside the pressable.

items.text: Use PressableFeedback to give press feedback to something that is not a button yet, such as a tile, a card or a row. Buttons and icon buttons already react to a press.
Pass `asChild` when the child is already a button or a link. Without it you nest a `<button>` inside a `<button>`, which is invalid HTML.
Handle the action with `onPress`. With `asChild` the child's own `onClick` still runs first, then `onPress`.
Give the pressable its look yourself: a border, a fill and a hover tone such as `hover:bg-bg-page`. The component only adds the scale, the opacity and the focus ring.
Don't put links or other buttons inside it without `asChild`. The content then sits inside a `<button>`, so nested interactive elements break.
Don't use it for a disabled state or for a name that is not in the content. The own button takes no `disabled` or `aria-label`; use `asChild` and put them on the child.
Don't use it on a large surface, such as a whole panel. A 5 % scale of a wide element moves its edges by a visible amount.

components.title: Emoji Reaction Button
components.description: A toggleable emoji reaction with a count, like a Slack reaction.

parts.name: EmojiReactionButton
parts.description: A native `<button>` with `aria-pressed` that shows an emoji and a count. It is controlled: you hold `active` and the count and change them in `onToggle`.

parts.name: Pill
parts.description: The 26 px high capsule: a 1 px border, a fully rounded shape and a small gap between emoji and count. Off, it has a neutral border and secondary text; on, an indigo tint with an indigo border and text.

parts.name: Emoji
parts.description: The emoji character, set at the text size of the pill. It is part of the button's accessible name, so a screen reader reads the emoji and then the count.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: The number of people who reacted, shown as a plain number after the emoji. It does not change by itself when the button is pressed: update it in `onToggle`.

items.text: Keep `active` and `count` in the same state and change them together in `onToggle`: turning on adds one, turning off takes one away.
Show only the reactions that exist, and open an Emoji Picker from a small icon button for the rest. A reaction that drops to zero should disappear.
Group the buttons in a row with `flex flex-wrap gap-2`, so they wrap on a narrow screen instead of overflowing.
Don't use it as a general toggle. It is for a reaction with a count; for an on or off option in a toolbar use Toggle.
Don't show a count of zero. A reaction nobody has chosen is not shown, and the Emoji Picker adds it again.
Don't use an emoji as the only information. Where the meaning matters, say it in text near the buttons.

components.title: Emoji Picker
components.description: A grid of selectable emoji, typically shown inside a Popover.

parts.name: EmojiPicker
parts.description: A panel with a grid of emoji buttons, in a `role="group"` named `Emoji`. It is a plain component with no state: `onSelect` receives the emoji that was pressed and you decide what happens next.

parts.name: Panel
parts.description: The card around the grid: a border, the popover surface, a shadow and 16 px corners. It holds six columns with 4 px between them and 8 px of padding, so a row of six buttons is 230 px wide.

parts.name: Emoji button
parts.description: A 32 px button with 8 px corners. Its accessible name is the emoji itself, which a screen reader announces by name. Hover fills it with `bg-page`, pressed with `bg-subtle`, and keyboard focus shows the indigo border and 2 px ring.

items.text: Put the picker inside a Popover that opens from an icon button, and close the Popover in `onSelect`. The picker draws its own card, so give the PopoverContent no box (`border-none bg-transparent p-0 shadow-none`).
Pass a short `emojis` array in a fixed order. The grid has six columns, so 6, 12 or 18 emoji fill every row.
Give the trigger an accessible name such as `Add a reaction`. The picker names its own buttons by their emoji, but the button that opens it needs words.
Don't use it as an emoji keyboard. It shows only the emoji you pass: no search, no categories, no skin tones and no recently used.
Don't use an emoji as the only information in a control. The buttons are named by the emoji alone, so keep visible text where the meaning matters.
Don't expect it to close anything. The picker does not know about the Popover it sits in, so a pick leaves the Popover open until you close it.

components.title: Timeline Event
components.description: One entry in an activity feed or history, with an avatar or status dot and a line to the next entry.

props.name: avatar
props.type: { src?: string; initials?: string; color?: AvatarColor }
props.description: Actor avatar (Type=event).

props.name: badge
props.description: Trailing badge/label on the title row (Type=step).

props.name: children
props.description: Extra content below the title (comment excerpt, reactions, attachments …).

props.name: last
props.description: Draw the connector line to the next entry.

props.name: object
props.description: Small object chip under the title (Type=event) — e.g. project name.

props.name: status
props.description: Status dot (Type=step): tone + icon.

parts.name: TimelineEvent
parts.description: One entry of an activity feed or a history: a mark on the left, a line down to the next entry, and the text on the right. Stack several in a column; each draws its own line.

parts.name: Avatar or status mark
parts.description: An Avatar from `avatar`, or a round status mark from `status` with a tone and an icon, a check by default. If both are set, the avatar wins.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title`, a sentence in secondary text. Text in `<strong>` stands out in the foreground colour, so the names read first.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The `time` at the right end of the title row, in small tertiary text, printed as written.

parts.name: Object chip
parts.description: A small chip under the title from `object`, naming what the event concerns, with a folder icon unless you pass `icon`.

parts.name: Connector
parts.description: The 2 px line from the mark to the next entry. It is green under a `success` status, grey otherwise, and left out when `last` is set.

parts.name: Badge
parts.description: A pill from `badge` and `badgeColor` on the right of the title row, for a status or an amount. It sits where the time sits, and both can be set.

parts.name: Meta and content
parts.description: The `meta` line in small tertiary text under the title, and the `children` below it for a comment excerpt, reactions or attachments.

items.text: Write the title as a sentence and wrap the names in ``: `Priya Raman moved Q4 report to Done`.
Name the person in the title. The avatar image is decorative and has an empty `alt`, so the title is all screen readers get.
Keep one kind in a list: avatars for what people did, status marks for the steps of a process such as an invoice or a release.
Set `last` on the final entry. Without it the line runs on into empty space below the feed.
Put long text in `children`, not in the title. A comment excerpt, a reaction row or a file goes under the title and the chip.
Don't let the tone carry the result alone. A warning mark has no text, so say `Changes requested` in the title or the badge as well.
Don't use Timeline Event for a plain sequence drawn from data, such as the stops of a parcel. A Timeline is shorter to write and takes `items`.
Don't put buttons or links in the title. Put them in `children`, where they sit under the sentence and keep their own focus order.

components.title: Avatar Stack
components.description: Overlapping avatars with a “+N” count for everyone past the limit.

parts.name: AvatarStack
parts.description: Shows the first `max` people, three by default, as avatars that overlap by 4 px and are ringed in the card colour. A `+N` avatar stands for the rest.

parts.name: Person
parts.description: One entry of `people`: a photo from `src`, or initials from `initials` or from the first letters of `name`, tinted in `color`, indigo by default.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: A `+N` avatar of the same size, shown only when `people` holds more than `max`.

items.text: Use an Avatar Stack for a compact row of assignees or guests passed as data, such as on a task or a schedule row. To compose avatars by hand, with a hover effect or a count button, use Avatar Group.
Pass the full `people` list and let `max` cut it. The `+N` count is worked out from what is left over.
Give every person a `name`. It is the hover title of the avatar and the source of the initials when there is no `src` or `initials`.
Write the names or the number beside the stack when it matters who is in it. The stack has no label of its own.
Keep the same `size` across one list, so the rows line up.
Don't place the stack on a tinted or muted background without checking it. The rings that separate the faces are drawn in the card colour, not in the colour behind.
Don't use a stack for people someone can open or choose. It is not interactive: use Avatar Group with an interactive count.

components.title: Agenda Event
components.description: One event in an agenda list, with its start and end time, a color bar, details and guests.

parts.name: AgendaEvent
parts.description: One row of a schedule with a line below it. With `onClick`, the title becomes a `<button>` stretched over the whole row and the row gets a hover fill and a focus ring.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The `start` time above an optional `end` time, in a fixed 64 px column. Both are printed as written.

parts.name: Colour bar
parts.description: A 3 px bar in the event `color`, one of eight hues, `purple` by default. It is always shown.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title`, up to two lines, then an ellipsis. With `onClick` it is a native `<button>` named by the title.

parts.name: Details
parts.description: The `meta` line under the title, in smaller tertiary text, such as the room or the call link. It is truncated to one line.

parts.name: Guests
parts.description: The `guests` as overlapping avatars: the first three, then a `+N` count for the rest.

parts.name: Menu button
parts.description: A small ghost icon button named `Event menu`, shown when `onMenu` is set. It sits above the stretched title, so its click does not open the event.

items.text: Use an Agenda Event for a schedule row with guests, a menu or a detail view to open. For a plain read-only list of times and titles, use Agenda.
Pass `onClick` instead of wrapping the row in a link or button. The title turns into a real button over the whole row, and the menu button stays reachable on its own.
Keep `title` short and put the place or the call details in `meta`. Both lines are cut to one line with an ellipsis.
Give every guest a `name`. It becomes the avatar's hover title and the source of the initials when there is no `src`.

Put the rows in a bordered, rounded container, remove the last line with `[&>*:last-child]:border-b-0` and round the first and last row with `[&>*:first-child]:rounded-t-xl` and `[&>*:last-child]:rounded-b-xl`. Each row draws its own line below, so the last one would double the border.
Don't let the colour bar carry the meaning alone. The bar has no text, so name the kind of event in `title` or `meta` as well.
Don't add `overflow-hidden` to the container. It clips the focus ring of a row, which is drawn on the outside of the row.
Don't put buttons or links inside `title` or `meta`. With `onClick` the title is already a button, and a control inside a button is invalid HTML; use `onMenu` for extra actions.

components.title: Form Actions
components.description: The row of buttons at the end of a form, aligned right, left or spread to both edges.

parts.name: FormActions
parts.description: The row, a `div` that lays its children out with 8 px between them and wraps them onto a second line on a narrow screen. `align` sets where the row sits: `end` (the default), `start` or `between`.

parts.name: Secondary action
parts.description: The way out of the form: Cancel, Discard or Back. A `plain` Button, so it reads as a normal action and not as the main one. It is disabled while the main action is pending.

parts.name: Main action
parts.description: The Button that sends the form: `type="submit"` with `variant="gradient"`. Its `phase` shows pending, success or error, and its label says what is happening. There is one per row.

parts.name: Destructive action
parts.description: An action that loses something, such as Delete draft. It sits at the other edge of the row (`align="between"`), so a quick tap on the main action cannot land on it. It is a plain Button; the irreversible step needs a confirmation of its own.

items.text: Use Form Actions for the buttons that end a form, a dialog, a sheet or a step. Buttons that act on the page and not on the form belong in a Toolbar.
Put the main action at the end of the row, next to the way out: `Cancel`, then `Save changes`. Write both as verbs that say what happens: `Create project`, not `OK`.
Keep the DOM order equal to the order on screen. At the end the main action is last; with `align="start"` it is first. Tab then follows what the eye sees.
Show a running send on the main action with `phase="pending"` and its own label (`Saving…`), and disable the way out while it runs. Show `Saved` with `phase="success"` for a moment afterwards.
Put a destructive action at the opposite edge with `align="between"`, and group the other two in a `div`. For an irreversible delete, ask in an Alert Dialog first.
Use the size of the fields above the row: 32, 36 or 40 px, one size for every button in it.
Don't give a row two gradient buttons. One main action per row; the second is a plain Button.
Don't hide the main action under a menu, and don't disable it without saying why. If there is nothing to save, say so in a status line.
Don't reorder the buttons with CSS `order` or `flex-row-reverse` to move the main action. The tab order stays the same and no longer matches the screen.

hooks.name: useDensity
hooks.summary: Reads and changes the density of the nearest DensityProvider.
hooks.description: Density sets the size of controls, fields and rows: `compact` (the default, controls 32–48 px) or `comfortable` (36–56 px). `useDensity` returns the density the nearest `DensityProvider` applies and a setter for it, so a settings page can offer the switch.

properties.name: density
properties.description: `"compact"` or `"comfortable"`: the density the provider applies to the document.

properties.name: setDensity
properties.description: Changes the density for the whole document. When the provider persists, the choice is written to localStorage as well. Calling it with the current value does nothing visible.

notes: Outside a `DensityProvider` it returns `compact` and a setter that does nothing.
The provider sets `data-density` on `<html>`, so portals such as menus and dialogs follow it. For one region only, wrap it in `<Density value>` instead.
With a `storageKey` on the provider the choice is kept in localStorage. Add `densityScript()` to the document head, so a stored `comfortable` paints before the first frame.
Switching density changes the layout without animation: the provider pauses transitions for one frame.

examples.title: A density setting
examples.description: A settings row that switches the whole document. The form below it reads the same tokens as every other control.

examples.title: Keep the choice without a flash
examples.description: The provider stores the choice. `densityScript()` applies it in the document head, before the first paint.

examples.title: Control the density yourself
examples.description: Pass `density` and `onDensityChange` to keep the value in your own state, a user profile or the URL. The hook then reports and requests changes.

hooks.name: useScrollSpy
hooks.summary: Tells which section of a page or a scroll container is being read.
hooks.description: Pass the ids of the section headings. The hook returns the id of the last section whose top has passed the reading line, a quarter down the window or the container, and a setter to move the marker yourself. At the end of the scroll the last section wins, so a short closing section still becomes active.
hooks.signature: useScrollSpy(ids: string[], root?: React.RefObject<HTMLElement | null> | undefined, enabled?: boolean): readonly [string | undefined, React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<string | undefined>>]

params.name: ids
params.description: The ids of the section elements, in the order they appear on the page. An id without an element in the page is ignored.

params.name: root
params.description: A ref to the element that scrolls the sections. Leave it out when the page itself scrolls. The sections are looked up inside this element, and the reading line is a quarter of its height from its top.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Set it to `false` to stop listening, for example while the list is hidden. The marker keeps its last value.

properties.name: active
properties.description: The id of the section being read. Before the first measurement it is the first id.

properties.name: setActive
properties.description: Moves the marker yourself, usually in the click handler of a list item. The next scroll measures again and takes over.

notes: `FloatingToc` uses it when you leave out `activeId`; reach for the hook when you build your own navigation.
Pass a ref as `root` when the sections scroll inside a container instead of the window.
`enabled={false}` stops listening, for example while a drawer that holds the list is closed.
Call the setter on click so the marker moves at once, before the smooth scroll arrives.

examples.title: Inside a scroll container
examples.description: A settings panel that scrolls on its own. `root` points at the panel, so the sections are looked up inside it and the reading line is a quarter of its height.

examples.title: Track the page
examples.description: Without `root` the hook watches the window, for a long article with a table of contents beside it.

examples.title: Pause while the list is hidden
examples.description: A drawer holds the section list. While it is closed nobody sees the marker, so the hook stops listening.

hooks.name: useToast
hooks.summary: Shows, updates and closes toasts from anywhere below a Toaster.
hooks.description: Returns the toast manager of the nearest `Toaster`. Call `add` with a title, an optional description and a type, and the toast slides into the corner the Toaster was given. `add` returns the toast's id, which `update` and `close` take.

properties.name: toasts
properties.description: The toasts that are open right now, newest first. The component re-renders whenever the list changes.

properties.name: add
properties.description: Shows a toast and returns its id. Options: `title`, `description`, `type` (`success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`), `timeout` in ms (`0` keeps it open), `priority` (`low` or `high`), `actionProps` for an inline action such as Undo, `onClose`, `onRemove` and `id`. Adding with an id that is already open updates that toast and restarts its timer.

properties.name: close
properties.description: Closes the toast with that id. Without an id it closes every open toast.

properties.name: update
properties.type: <T extends Data = Data>(toastId: string, options: ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T> | ((prevToast: ToastObject<T>) => ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T>)) => void
properties.description: Changes an open toast in place: pass the fields to change, or a function that gets the previous toast and returns them. The toast keeps its place in the stack.

properties.name: promise
properties.type: <Value, T extends Data = Data>(promise: Promise<Value>, options: ToastManagerPromiseOptions<Value, T>) => Promise<Value>
properties.description: Shows the `loading` toast, then turns it into `success` or `error` when the promise settles. Each state is a title string or the same options as `add`; `success` and `error` can be functions of the result. Returns the promise, so you can await it.

notes: Mount `Toaster` once, high in the tree (the root layout). Without it, `add` has nowhere to render.
`type` sets the colour of the dot: `success`, `error`, `warning` or `info` (the default).
Toasts close after 5 seconds. Pass `timeout` to keep one longer, or `0` to keep it until it is closed.
Use a toast to confirm something that already happened. A decision the user still has to make belongs in a Dialog.

examples.title: Confirm an action
examples.description: A form that saves and tells the person it worked. The toast confirms what already happened.

examples.title: Follow a request
examples.description: `promise` shows a loading toast and turns it into the result, so one call covers all three states.

examples.title: Update a toast in place
examples.description: `add` returns the id of the toast. A `timeout` of `0` keeps it open while the work runs; `update` then turns it into the result.

durations.use: Tooltip dismiss, press release. Barely reads as motion.
The default exit. Hover, focus ring, checkbox, switch track.
Dropdown, popover, context menu, backdrop, collapse.
Dialog, toast, switch thumb — a surface arriving.
A side panel and a full-width panel. Rare.
Progress and meter fills. Data moving, not chrome.

easings.use: Anything arriving. Fast start, long settle. The house curve.
Anything repositioning while staying on screen.
Dialog, popover, switch. At most one per screen.
A sampled spring: one soft overshoot, then it settles. Something physical landing — a thumb, an arrow, a released sheet. Never on a data value.

amplitudes.use: Tooltip — stays glued to its anchor.

rules: **Duration and easing are class names, not numbers.** `duration-base`, `ease-entrance`. Tailwind has no `--duration-*` theme namespace, so WunderUI ships these as `@utility` rules that also set `--tw-duration` — which means they work on `animate-in` / `animate-out` too.
**Only `transform` and `opacity`.** Everything else goes through layout or paint. Height animates via `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`, never via `height`.
**Entrances decelerate, exits accelerate.** `ease-entrance` in, `ease-exit` out — and the exit is one step shorter on the duration scale, never the entrance duration reversed.
**Never fade in the LCP element.** An element at `opacity: 0` is not an LCP candidate, so a 600ms hero fade adds 600ms to your LCP. Render headline copy at full opacity; animate `transform` only.
**Restrain the travel.** Anything anchored to a trigger moves `--travel-xs` or `--travel-sm`. A menu that slides 20px looks like it fell in.

**One overshoot per screen.** `ease-overshoot` is punctuation. Two of them on one view and the interface reads as a toy. Never on a data value: a bar, gauge or bubble that swings past its number shows a wrong number for a moment.

**Reduced motion is opt-in, not a kill switch.** Wrap the animation in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` so the still state is the default and you cannot forget a selector. Reduced means calmer, not nothing: drop transforms and travel, keep opacity and colour changes (rule 15).

**Never `transition-all`.** Name the properties — `transition-[opacity,transform]` — or use bare `transition`, which covers colour, shadow, transform and opacity but no layout property. `transition-all` animates things you did not mean to animate, including on first paint.
**Loading keeps its height.** A skeleton occupies the same box as the content it stands in for, and crossfades — it never collapses and reflows.
**A looping ambient animation is the one place `ease-in-out` belongs.** A shimmer that runs forever has no entrance and no exit, so symmetry is correct there and nowhere else.

**Animate by frequency.** Keyboard-driven and 100+/day actions (command palette, shortcuts, moving between tooltips) get no motion; tens a day get a short fade; rare moments may delight. Tooltips skip their entrance when another one was just open (`data-open:data-instant:animate-none`).

**Anchored surfaces grow from their trigger.** Popover, dropdown, tooltip, hover card and select use `origin-(--transform-origin)`. Never start from `scale(0)` — start at 0.92–0.97 with opacity. Centred dialogs are exempt.

**Toggles stay interruptible.** Animate switches, checkboxes, tabs and other repeated state changes with transitions — they retarget from wherever they are — never with keyframes bound to the state, which restart from zero. An overshoot transition (`transition-transform duration-base ease-overshoot`) still swings past the end.

**Hover only where hover exists.** Tailwind v4's `hover:` is already gated to `(hover: hover)`; hand-written `:hover` in CSS goes inside `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`, so a tap on a phone does not leave a hover state stuck.

**Reduced motion keeps the fade.** WunderUI's global rule zeroes the scale, slide, spin and blur of every `animate-in` / `animate-out` and every transform transition, and keeps opacity and colour — so do not add `motion-reduce:transition-none` or `motion-reduce:animate-none` to a fade.

recipes.Overlay enter and exit:
/* Dialog, sheet, popover, dropdown, context menu — one pattern for all of them.
   Base UI exposes data-open / data-closed; tw-animate-css turns them into keyframes. */
<Dialog.Popup className="
  data-open:animate-in   data-open:fade-in-0   data-open:zoom-in-92
  data-open:slide-in-from-bottom-2
  data-open:duration-slow  data-open:ease-overshoot
  data-closed:animate-out  data-closed:fade-out-0 data-closed:zoom-out-96
  data-closed:duration-fast data-closed:ease-exit
" />

topics.title: Installation
topics.summary: Install the package or add the source, wire up the styles and the @source path.

topics.title: Rules for agents
topics.summary: The rules every screen follows: tokens, theming, imports, composites, motion.
topics.body:
1. **Never hardcode colours.** Every value is a CSS variable. Use the Tailwind utility that maps to it (`bg-card`, `text-text-secondary`, `border-border`), not a hex.
2. **Theme by overriding tokens**, not by restyling components. Setting `--primary` on any wrapper re-themes everything inside it.
3. **Dark mode is a `.dark` class on `<html>`.** `ThemeProvider` (next-themes) handles it. Never write your own dark colours.
4. **The package is client code.** It ships with a `"use client"` banner, so you can import it inside React Server Components, but its own components run on the client.
5. **Import from the package root**, never from `dist/` or `src/` paths.
6. `cn` is not re-exported — import it from the `cn` package directly.
7. **Prefer a composite over rebuilding one.** Before writing a table, a board, a stat row or a chat bubble by hand, check the task table and the inventory below — it probably exists.
8. **Charts take a `loading` prop**; do not build your own skeleton.
10. **Motion comes from tokens too.** Duration is `duration-instant|fast|base|slow|deliberate|ambient`, easing is `ease-entrance|exit|move|overshoot|spring`. Never write a raw `duration-300` and never write `ease-in-out` — both are the default every generator reaches for, and both read as mechanical.

topics.title: Task → component
topics.summary: Which component to use for a task — look here before building anything by hand.
topics.body:
Look here first. Most requests map to something that already exists.

| I need … | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Plain table markup, no behaviour | `Table` and its parts |
| Editable cells inside a table | `CellSelect`, `CellSwitch`, `CellSlider`, `CellColorPicker` |
| Formatted table cells | `UserCell`, `BadgeCell`, `CurrencyCell`, `ProgressCell`, `TagCell`, `RatingCell` |
| Bulk actions for a selection | `ActionBar` |
| A percentage change as a small pill | `TrendChip` |
| Modal for a focused task | `Dialog` |
| Confirmation with consequences | `AlertDialog` |
| Text input that suggests while typing | `Combobox` or `Autocomplete` |
| Pick a date | `DatePicker`, or `Calendar` for an inline month |
| Form with labels and validation | `Form` + `Field` + `Fieldset` |
| Settings row with a toggle | `SelectorItem` + `Switch`, grouped in `SelectorItemGroup` |
| Switch between views, compactly | `Segment`; `Tabs` when the views are panels |
| File upload | `DropZone` |
| Nothing to show yet | `EmptyState` |
| Something is loading | `Skeleton`; charts take `loading` |
| Transient notification | `useToast` with `Toaster`; `Alert` when it should stay |
| Chronological events | `Timeline`; `Agenda` for scheduled ones |
| Folder and file tree | `FileTree` |
| Time an interaction | `duration-fast` hover/press and every exit · `duration-base` menus · `duration-slow` dialogs · `duration-deliberate` sheets · `duration-ambient` data bars |
| Ease an interaction | `ease-entrance` arriving · `ease-exit` leaving · `ease-move` repositioning · `ease-overshoot` once per screen at most |
| Animate something open or closed | `data-open` / `data-closed` variants; height via `grid-rows-[0fr]` → `[1fr]` |

### Gradients

Figma `Gradient/<Hue>` paint styles as `bg-gradient-<hue>` (blue, yellow, red, indigo, purple,
pink, orange, green, alternative), plus `bg-gradient-dark` (gradient/start → end),
`bg-gradient-slate` (start-2 → end-2) and `bg-gradient-primary` (start-3 → brand-primary).

Figma `Gradient Ramp/<Hue>` paint styles as `bg-gradient-ramp-<hue>` (the same nine hues): four stops
`<hue>/300` at 0 %, `/400` at 40 %, `/500` at 65 % and `/600` at 100 %, linear, dark at the top and light at the
bottom, every stop a primitive (`--<hue>-300` … `--<hue>-600`). Use a ramp for a large surface that needs depth; keep `bg-gradient-<hue>` for small tiles and logos.

### Effects

Figma Shadow styles on the Tailwind scale: `shadow-xs` Small (0 1 2 / 5%), `shadow-sm` Regular
(0 2 4 / 8%), `shadow-md` Medium (0 4 8 / 10%), `shadow-lg` Large (0 8 16 / 12%), `shadow-xl`
XLarge (0 16 32 -4 / 16%). Shadow colours: `--effect-shadow`, `--effect-shadow-2`, `--effect-shadow-3`.

### Radius

| Token | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `--radius` | `0.75rem` |

### Typography

Font family comes from the host app through `--font-sans`; WunderUI maps
`--font-heading` to the same stack. The documentation site uses Inter.

### Density

Compact is the default: controls are 32, 36, 40, 44 and 48 px (`sm` to `2xl`), one scale for
buttons and fields, text stays 14 px. `data-density="comfortable"` on `<html>` or any ancestor
restores the roomier sizes (36 to 56 px); it nests in both directions. In code: `<Density value>`,
`DensityProvider` and `useDensity()`. Do not hard-code control heights (`h-9`, `h-11`) — use
the component sizes so density keeps working. Portals (menus, dialogs) read the page's density.

### Icons

Lucide (`lucide-react`) is the icon set of every component, block and dashboard. The Solar icon set
(1,451 icons in six styles: linear, line-duotone, bold, bold-duotone, broken, outline) is for templates and block
variations: `import { SolarBell } from "@wunderui/react/icons/solar/bell"`, then
`<SolarBell variant="bold-duotone" className="size-5" />`. Every export starts with `Solar`. Do not mix the two
sets on one surface; Solar has no plain close glyph, use Lucide's `X`. Credit: Solar Icon Set by 480 Design
(CC BY 4.0), modified; keep it with your third-party notices.

### Spacing

One spacing system for dashboards, templates and blocks, on a 4-px base. Use only these steps:
2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48. The gap inside a group is smaller than the gap between groups.
Desktop means `lg` (1024 px) and up; card padding switches at `md` (768 px).

| Area | Desktop | Mobile | Tailwind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Top bar | none, the page header sits in the content | 56, padding 12 / 12 / 12 / 16, bottom border | `h-14` |
| Page padding left and right | 32 | 16 | `px-4 lg:px-8` |
| Page padding top / bottom | 32 / 48 | 32 / 48 | `pt-8 pb-12` |
| Page title → supporting text | 2 | 2 | `gap-0.5` |
| Title block → tabs or filters (tabs start the next section) | 32 | 32 | `gap-8` |
| Tabs or filters → their content (same section) | 16 | 16 | `gap-4` |
| Buttons in an action row | 8 | 8 | `gap-2` |
| Gap between sections | 32 | 32 | `gap-8` |
| Section header → content | 16 (header: 16 bottom padding, bottom border) | 16 | `gap-4`, `pb-4 border-b` |
| Card gap | 24 | 20 | `gap-5 lg:gap-6` |
| Cards in a KPI row | 16 | 16 | `gap-4` |
| Main column ↔ right rail (a card gap) | 24 | 24, stacked | `gap-6` |
| Card padding (every card) | 16 | 16 | `p-4` |
| Card inner gap | 16 | 16 | `gap-4` |
| Card radius | 16 | 16 | `rounded-xl` |
| KPI label → value → trend | 8 → 8 | 8 → 8 | `gap-2` |
| Tables | in their card | full bleed, no radius | `-mx-4 rounded-none lg:mx-0 lg:rounded-xl` |

Three card types: modal card (sign-in, sign-up, verification; stands alone on a screen or in a modal) with padding 48 top and bottom and 40 left and right; standard card (KPI, chart, widget and everything else) with padding 16 and inner gap 16; table / list card with padding 16, List Panel rows 8 px from the card edge. Auth card gaps: title → subtitle 8, header → first
field 24, label → input 8, input → helper 4, field → field 20, last field → primary button 24,
button → divider → alternatives 24 and 24, stacked buttons 8.

### Component spacing

Gaps inside components follow one scale too: label → control 8 (`gap-2`), control → helper, caption or error 4 (`gap-1`), field → field in a form or dialog 20 (`gap-5`), icon → label in items (buttons, menu and nav rows, breadcrumb, stepper, tree, notification, chips, pills, tags, segment options) 8, buttons side by side or stacked 8 (button icons are 16 px, 18 px at the default `md` size), header → content (collapsible, popover, dialog, table caption, toolbar filters) 16, title → description 4 (modal, auth and alert dialog 8; dense two-line rows 2), nav rows 4, every card padding 16, inner gap 16, radius 16. Build the label and the helper as siblings of the control in one column with `gap-1` and give the label `mb-1`.
